iarbas.s: Iarbas was a legendary Berber king in North Africa associated with the founding of Carthage. In the tradition, Elissa, known as Dido, negotiated with him for as much land as an ox-hide could cover and cut the hide into strips to encircle the hill of Byrsa.

ibadan.s: Ibadan is a city in south-western Nigeria. It grew rapidly in the nineteenth century as refugees and warriors settled there after the collapse of the Oyo Empire.

iberia.s: Iberia, or the Iberian Peninsula, is the south-western peninsula of Europe, comprising Spain and Portugal. It was a major arena for Carthage, conquered by the Umayyad Caliphate and later ruled by the Almoravid Empire and the Almohad Caliphate.

iberian-union.s: The Iberian Union was the dynastic union of the crowns of Portugal and Spain under the Spanish Habsburg kings, beginning in 1580 and lasting until 1640. Portugal kept its own institutions but was drawn into Spain's wars.

ibn-battuta.s: Ibn Battuta was a fourteenth-century Moroccan traveller whose account of his journeys across Africa and Asia is a major historical source. He served at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq in Delhi between 1334 and 1341, including as a judge.

ibn-hawqal.s: Ibn Hawqal was a tenth-century Arab geographer and traveller. Writing around c.

ibn-tumart.s: Ibn Tumart was a Berber religious reformer who preached a strict doctrine of the unity of God and proclaimed himself the Mahdi. From the Atlas Mountains he led a movement against the Almoravid Empire, and died in 1130.

ibrahim-lodi.s: Ibrahim Lodi was the last sultan of the Lodi dynasty and of the Delhi Sultanate. He was defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

ibrahim-of-darfur.s: Ibrahim was a sultan of Darfur who died in 1874. In October that year he was defeated at the Battle of Manawashi by the forces of al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur, a slave-trading warlord backed by Egypt.

ibrahim-shah.s: Ibrahim Shah was a nephew of Nader Shah and briefly a ruler of the Afsharid state. He fought a civil war against his brother Adil Shah in 1747–1748 after Nader's assassination.

idris-alooma.s: Idris Alooma was a mai, or king, of Bornu who reigned c. 1571–1603.

idris-al-wathiq.s: Idris al-Wathiq was the last Almohad caliph, who by then controlled only Marrakesh. He was murdered in 1269, and the Marinids seized the city.

idris-i-al-mamun.s: Idris I al-Mamun was an Almohad caliph of the early thirteenth century. In 1229 he renounced Ibn Tumart's status as Mahdi, abandoning a founding doctrine of the Almohad movement.

idrisid-dynasty.s: The Idrisid dynasty was the first Islamic dynasty to rule Morocco, founded in the late eighth century. Early Arab writers used it as a point of comparison for the Ghana Empire: the astronomer al-Fazari described Ghana as equal in size to the Idrisid state.

ifat-sultanate.s: The Ifat Sultanate was a Muslim state in the eastern Ethiopian region, ruled by the Walashma dynasty from the late thirteenth century. It came into conflict with the Christian Ethiopian kingdom and was defeated.

ife.s: Ife is an ancient city in south-western Nigeria, regarded as the spiritual birthplace of the Yoruba people and renowned for its bronze and terracotta sculpture. Benin traditions link the founding of the Oba dynasty to a prince from Ife.

ifriqiya.s: Ifriqiya was the medieval Arabic name for the region roughly corresponding to present-day Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya. The Fatimid Caliphate was founded there in the early tenth century before moving to Egypt.

igala.s: The Igala are a people of central Nigeria, east of the Niger–Benue confluence, whose kingdom was a regional power. In the early sixteenth century they invaded Benin from the north.

igbesanmwan.s: The Igbesanmwan were the royal guild of ivory carvers in the Benin kingdom. Like other craft guilds, they worked for the Oba and lived in their own quarter of Benin City.

igue-festival.s: The Igue festival is an annual royal festival in Benin City, held at the end of the year to renew the spiritual power of the Oba and bless the kingdom. It forms part of the cycle of royal rituals centred on the king.

igun-eronmwon.s: The Igun Eronmwon were the royal guild of bronze casters in the Benin kingdom, working under the patronage of the Oba. They produced the cast brass and bronze works known as the Benin Bronzes.

ijaye.s: Ijaye was a Yoruba town in south-western Nigeria that grew as a military and refugee centre after the collapse of the Oyo Empire. It was one of the new powers that emerged in the nineteenth-century Yoruba wars.

ijtihad.s: Ijtihad is the Islamic legal concept of independent reasoning by a qualified scholar to reach a ruling where scripture does not give a clear answer. It played an important part in the development of Islamic law.

ili-river.s: The Ili River flows from the Tian Shan mountains into Lake Balkhash in Central Asia. Its valley provided rich pastures and was the political heartland of the Chagatai Khanate.

ilkhan.s: Ilkhan was the title adopted by Hulagu and his successors, meaning a subordinate khan. It acknowledged the nominal supremacy of the Great Khan in Mongolia.

ilkhanate.s: The Ilkhanate was a Mongol state founded by Hulagu Khan in the mid-thirteenth century, ruling Iran, Iraq and neighbouring lands. Its rulers later converted to Islam, and under Ghazan carried out major reforms.

ilorin.s: Ilorin is a city in west-central Nigeria that was originally a provincial centre of the Oyo Empire. Its revolt in the early nineteenth century, followed by its incorporation into the Sokoto Caliphate, contributed to the collapse of Oyo.

ilorin-emirate.s: The Ilorin Emirate was the southernmost emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate, established in the former Oyo province of Ilorin. It became a base for the caliphate's expansion into Yoruba lands.

ilterish-qaghan.s: Ilterish Qaghan was a Turkic leader who revived Gokturk independence from Tang China in 682 CE. Starting with a small band of followers in the Yin Shan mountains, he rebuilt the Second Turkic Khaganate through guerrilla warfare.

iltutmish.s: Iltutmish was a Turkic slave commander who seized the throne of Delhi in 1211. He consolidated the sultanate and in 1229 was recognised by the Abbasid caliph as Sultan of Hindustan.

ilum-ma-ili.s: Ilum-ma-ili was the founder of the Sealand Dynasty in southern Mesopotamia. After defeating Samsu-iluna, the son of Hammurabi, he broke the south away from Babylonian control.

ilunga-kabale.s: Ilunga Kabale was a ruler of the Luba kingdom in central Africa, whose reign of c. 1840–1870 belonged to the empire's period of greatest extent.

ilunga-sungu.s: Ilunga Sungu was a ruler of the Luba kingdom in central Africa, reigning c. 1780–1810.

imam.s: An imam is a Muslim religious leader, ranging from the leader of congregational prayer to, in Shia Islam, the divinely guided head of the community. The Fatimid caliphs claimed to be imams in the Ismaili sense.

imamate.s: The imamate is the Shia doctrine of leadership of the Muslim community by imams descended from the Prophet Muhammad through Ali. Ismaili Shia belief held that a hidden imam would reappear.

immortals.s: The Immortals were an elite force of the Achaemenid Persian army, described by Herodotus as numbering ten thousand. According to him, any fallen or sick member was immediately replaced, keeping the unit at full strength.

imperator-romanorum.s: Imperator Romanorum, meaning Emperor of the Romans, was the imperial title revived in the West when Charlemagne was crowned by the pope in 800. It claimed continuity with the Roman Empire.

imperial-academy.s: The Imperial Academy, or Taixue, was an institution established under Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty in 124 BCE to train officials in the Confucian classics. It helped make Confucian learning the basis of government service.

imperial-and-royal-army.s: The Imperial and Royal Army was the common army of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, known by the abbreviation k.u.k. (kaiserlich und königlich).

imperial-chamber-court.s: The Imperial Chamber Court was one of the two supreme courts of the Holy Roman Empire, established in 1495 as part of imperial reform. It heard disputes between the empire's estates and appeals from lower courts.

imperial-diet.s: The Imperial Diet, or Reichstag, was the assembly of the estates of the Holy Roman Empire, including princes, ecclesiastical rulers and imperial cities. It dealt with matters such as taxation, war and law.

imperial-examination.s: The imperial examination was the system of competitive examinations, based largely on the Confucian classics, used in China to recruit government officials. It developed under the Sui and Tang Dynasty and became central under the Song Dynasty.

imperial-general-headquarters.s: The Imperial General Headquarters was the supreme command of the Japanese army and navy in wartime, operating under the emperor. It directed Japan's military operations during the Second World War.

imperial-overextension.s: Imperial overextension is a recurring pattern in which an empire expands beyond its capacity to defend, administer or finance its territories. Distant wars, long frontiers and costly garrisons drain resources and invite revolt or invasion.

impressionism.s: Impressionism was a nineteenth-century art movement, chiefly French, that sought to capture light and fleeting impressions of everyday scenes. Many Impressionists were influenced by Japanese woodblock prints, part of the Japonisme fashion.

inanna.s: Inanna was the Sumerian goddess of love, war and fertility, identified with the Akkadian Ishtar. Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess at Ur, composed hymns to her and is regarded as the first named author in history.

inca-empire.s: The Inca Empire was the largest state in pre-Columbian America, centred on Cusco in the Andes of South America. It was conquered by Spanish forces led by Francisco Pizarro from 1532.

incense.s: Incense is aromatic resin or plant material burned for its fragrance, especially in religious rituals. Frankincense and myrrh from north-east Africa and southern Arabia were highly valued in the ancient world.

india.s: India is a region of South Asia, home to some of the world's oldest civilisations and a long series of empires, including the Maurya, Gupta, Delhi Sultanate, Mughal, Maratha and Sikh states. Its wealth and trade drew the attention of many outside powers.

indian-army.s: The Indian Army was the army of British India, recruited largely from Indian soldiers under British officers. It policed India and served in campaigns across Asia, Africa and Europe, including both world wars.

indian-civil-service.s: The Indian Civil Service was the elite administrative service of British India, recruited by competitive examination. A small number of officials governed districts and provinces across the subcontinent.

indian-independence.s: Indian independence refers to the end of British rule in India in 1947, when the subcontinent was partitioned into India and Pakistan. It followed decades of nationalist struggle and the strains of the Second World War.

indian-national-congress.s: The Indian National Congress is a political party founded in 1885 that became the leading organisation of the Indian independence movement. Under leaders such as Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru it organised mass campaigns against British rule.

indian-ocean.s: The Indian Ocean is the world's third-largest ocean, bounded by Africa, Asia and Australia. Its monsoon winds made it one of the oldest and busiest arenas of long-distance maritime trade.

indian-ocean-trade.s: Indian Ocean trade refers to the maritime exchange of goods such as spices, textiles, gold, ivory and ceramics across the Indian Ocean, driven by seasonal monsoon winds. It connected East Africa, Arabia, the Persian Gulf, India and South-East Asia.

indian-rebellion-of-1857.s: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was a major uprising against the rule of the British East India Company, beginning with a mutiny of Indian soldiers. The rebels proclaimed the elderly Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II as their leader.

indian-subcontinent.s: The Indian subcontinent is the large region of South Asia comprising present-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and neighbouring lands. It has been home to empires such as the Maurya Empire and the Delhi Sultanate.

indigenat.s: The indigénat was a legal regime in the French colonial empire that subjected colonial subjects to separate administrative penalties, imposed by officials without trial. It applied to indigenous populations while French citizens lived under French law.

indigo.s: Indigo is a blue dye obtained from plants, widely used to colour textiles. In West Africa, indigo-dyed cloth was an important craft product.

indirect-rule.s: Indirect rule is a method of government in which an imperial power governs through existing local rulers and institutions rather than replacing them. The Gupta Empire ruled a wide periphery of tributary kings in this way, and the Dutch and Italian empires relied on local elites.

indo-aryans.s: The Indo-Aryans are speakers of the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European languages, which includes Sanskrit. In the Mitanni Empire, a ruling elite with Indo-Aryan names and deities governed a largely Hurrian population.

indochina.s: Indochina, or French Indochina, was the federation of French colonial territories in South-East Asia comprising Vietnam's three regions, Cambodia and Laos. It was governed by a governor-general from Hanoi.

indo-greek-kingdom.s: The Indo-Greek Kingdom was a group of Hellenistic states in north-western India and present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan, ruled by Greek kings from the second century BCE. It developed from the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom.

indo-islamic-culture.s: Indo-Islamic culture refers to the blend of Islamic, Persian and Indian traditions that developed in South Asia under Muslim rulers. It is visible in architecture, music, language and literature, including the growth of Urdu.

indonesia.s: Indonesia is an archipelago nation in South-East Asia comprising thousands of islands, including Java and Sumatra. Much of it was once under the influence of the Majapahit Empire.

indonesian-independence.s: Indonesian independence was proclaimed in 1945 and recognised by the Netherlands in 1949 after a period of armed conflict and negotiation. It ended Dutch rule over the East Indies.

indonesian-national-revolution.s: The Indonesian National Revolution was the armed and diplomatic struggle for independence from Dutch rule, fought from 1947 to 1949 in its main phase. The Netherlands launched two major military offensives, known as the Police Actions, but faced international pressure.

indo-persian-culture.s: Indo-Persian culture refers to the synthesis of Persian and Indian traditions that flourished in South Asia, especially at Muslim courts. Persian served as the language of administration and high literature, and Persian styles shaped painting and architecture.

indus.s: The Indus is a great river of South Asia flowing from Tibet through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. Its valley supported one of the earliest civilisations.

indus-valley.s: The Indus Valley is the region along the Indus River in present-day Pakistan and north-western India. In the Bronze Age it was home to the Indus Valley Civilisation, known to Mesopotamians as Meluhha.

indus-valley-civilisation.s: The Indus Valley Civilisation was a Bronze Age civilisation in the Indus basin, known for planned cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. It is generally identified with the land of Meluhha in Mesopotamian texts.

industrial-revolution.s: The Industrial Revolution was the transition to mechanised production, steam power and factory industry that began in Britain in the eighteenth century. It greatly increased Britain's productive and military capacity.

infaq-al-maysur.s: Infaq al-Maysur is a historical work by Muhammad Bello, the second ruler of the Sokoto Caliphate. It recounts the jihad of Usman dan Fodio and the early history of the caliphate.

inflation.s: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices, reducing the purchasing power of money. The Spanish Empire experienced the Price Revolution as American silver flowed into Europe.

inflation-and-currency-debasement.s: Inflation and currency debasement is a recurring pattern in which rulers reduce the precious-metal content of coins or over-issue paper money to meet expenses, leading to rising prices and loss of confidence. It can damage commerce, impoverish fixed-income groups and undermine…

ingria.s: Ingria is a historical region on the southern shore of the Gulf of Finland, around present-day St Petersburg. It was held by Sweden in the seventeenth century.

inner-asia.s: Inner Asia refers to the interior regions of Asia, including Mongolia, Manchuria, Xinjiang, Tibet and the Central Asian steppe. It was the home of nomadic empires such as the Xiongnu Empire.

inner-niger-delta.s: The Inner Niger Delta is a vast seasonal floodplain of the Niger River in present-day Mali. Its fertile land and waterways supported rice farming, fishing and trade, with cities such as Djenné.

institutes-of-justinian.s: The Institutes of Justinian is a textbook of Roman law completed in 533 CE as part of the codification ordered by the emperor Justinian I. It formed one part of the body of law later known as the Corpus Juris Civilis.

inter-caetera.s: Inter caetera is a papal bull issued by Pope Alexander VI in 1493, after Columbus's first voyage. It granted Castile rights over lands discovered to the west of a line in the Atlantic, dividing spheres of exploration with Portugal.

internal-rebellion.s: Internal rebellion is a recurring pattern in which revolts by peasants, provinces, generals or religious movements weaken or overthrow a ruling power. Rebellions often arise from heavy taxation, famine, misrule or ethnic grievances.

international-law.s: International law is the body of rules governing relations between states. Early precursors include the treaties of the Hittite Empire, which set out obligations between rulers.

international-monetary-fund.s: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international financial institution founded in 1944 to support monetary co-operation and provide emergency financing. During the Suez Crisis of 1956, the United States threatened to block IMF support for Britain unless it withdrew…

interpretatio-romana.s: Interpretatio romana was the Roman practice of identifying foreign gods with Roman deities, such as equating a Celtic god with Mercury or Mars. It allowed local cults to be absorbed within Roman religion.

ionia.s: Ionia was the central part of the western coast of Anatolia, settled by Ionian Greeks and home to cities such as Miletus and Ephesus. After Cyrus the Great defeated Croesus of Lydia in 546 BCE, the Ionian cities came under Achaemenid rule.

ipiranga-river.s: The Ipiranga is a small river, or stream, in São Paulo, Brazil. On its banks Prince Pedro made the declaration of independence from Portugal in 1822, known as the Grito do Ipiranga.

iqta.s: The iqta was an Islamic administrative system in which the right to collect revenue from a territory was assigned to military officers in place of salary. The Seljuk Empire used it widely to support its armies.

iran.s: Iran is a country and historical region of south-western Asia, centred on the Iranian plateau. It was the heartland of a long line of empires, including the Median, Achaemenid, Parthian and Sasanian empires, and later the Safavid, Afsharid and Zand states.

iranian-plateau.s: The Iranian plateau is a high region of south-western Asia lying between Mesopotamia, Central Asia and the Indus valley. It formed the geographical core of Iranian empires such as the Median, Achaemenid, Parthian and Sasanian empires.

iraq.s: Iraq is a region of south-western Asia centred on the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the land of ancient Mesopotamia. Its rich agricultural lands made it a prize for many empires, including the Sasanian Empire, the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates and the Ilkhanate.

iron-plough.s: The iron plough, or iron-tipped plough, is a plough whose cutting edge is made of iron, allowing deeper and more efficient tillage. In Han China, iron ploughs and improved irrigation increased agricultural yields.

iron-smelting.s: Iron smelting is the extraction of iron from ore by heating it in a furnace. The Kushite Empire was a notable centre of iron production, with Meroë often associated with large-scale smelting.

iron-technology.s: Iron technology refers to the production and use of iron for tools and weapons, which spread widely in the ancient Near East at the end of the Bronze Age. The Hittite Empire is associated with early ironworking.

iron-working.s: Iron working is the craft of smelting and forging iron to make tools and weapons. In West Africa, the Soninke founders of the Ghana Empire were iron-working people, giving them military and agricultural advantages.

ironclad.s: An ironclad was a steam-powered warship protected by iron or steel armour plates, developed in the mid-nineteenth century. During the Paraguayan War, the Brazilian Empire built a navy of modern ironclads.

irredentism.s: Irredentism is a political movement seeking to annex territories inhabited by people of the same ethnicity or regarded as historically belonging to a nation. After the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, its successor states left significant minorities across new borders.

irrigation-and-water-management.s: Irrigation and water management is a recurring pattern in which states rise and prosper by controlling water through canals, dams and underground channels to support agriculture and population. Neglect or failure of these systems can contribute to decline.

isabel-princess-imperial-of-brazil.s: Isabel, Princess Imperial of Brazil, was the daughter and heir of Emperor Pedro II. As regent in 1888, while her father was in Europe, she signed the Lei Áurea abolishing slavery in Brazil.

isabella-i-of-castile.s: Isabella I of Castile was Queen of Castile who, with her husband Ferdinand of Aragon, united the Spanish crowns. In 1492 they completed the Reconquista with the fall of Granada and sponsored Columbus's first voyage.

isfahan.s: Isfahan is a city in central Iran with a long history as a political and cultural centre. It was a capital under the Seljuk Empire and was rebuilt as the splendid capital of the Safavid Empire under Shah Abbas I.

ishaq-ibn-ali.s: Ishaq ibn Ali was the last ruler of the Almoravid dynasty, then still a young man. He was killed when the Almohad forces of Abd al-Mumin stormed Marrakesh in 1147.

ishtar-gate.s: The Ishtar Gate was a monumental gateway to the inner city of Babylon, built under Nebuchadnezzar II and dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. It was faced with blue glazed bricks decorated with dragons, bulls and lions.

isin.s: Isin was an ancient city in southern Mesopotamia. After the fall of the Neo-Sumerian Empire, its dynasty became one of the leading powers of the region, rivalling Larsa.

isin-dynasty.s: The Isin dynasty was a line of kings who ruled from the city of Isin in southern Mesopotamia after the collapse of the Third Dynasty of Ur. It claimed continuity with Ur's rulers and competed with the dynasty of Larsa.

islam.s: Islam is a monotheistic religion founded in Arabia in the seventh century CE through the teaching of the Prophet Muhammad, centred on the Quran. It shaped the founding and governance of many empires, from the Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates to the Ottoman, Safavid and…

islamic-calendar.s: The Islamic calendar is a lunar calendar of twelve months, dating its years from the Hijra of the Prophet Muhammad in 622 CE. It was introduced as an official dating system under the caliph Umar.

islamic-golden-age.s: The Islamic Golden Age refers to a period of flourishing science, philosophy, literature and art in the Islamic world, conventionally associated with the Abbasid Caliphate from the eighth century. Scholars in centres such as Baghdad translated and extended Greek, Persian and…

islamic-jurisprudence.s: Islamic jurisprudence, or fiqh, is the human understanding and elaboration of Islamic law derived from the Quran, the hadith and scholarly reasoning. It was developed by schools of law such as the Maliki and Hanafi.

islamisation.s: Islamisation refers to the process by which societies or rulers adopt Islam and Islamic institutions, through conversion, conquest, trade or reform. It occurred in different ways across the Umayyad Caliphate's conquests and the Seljuk Empire's Anatolia.

islamization.s: Islamisation, also spelled Islamization, is the process by which societies adopt Islam and Islamic institutions. In the Indonesian archipelago it spread through trade and the conversion of coastal rulers from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

ismail-i.s: Ismail I was the founder of the Safavid dynasty, who took Tabriz and was proclaimed shah in 1501. He made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, a decision with lasting consequences.

ismailism.s: Isma'ilism is a branch of Shia Islam that recognises Ismail, son of the imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and his descendants as the line of imams. The Fatimid Caliphate was founded on Ismaili claims and promoted the faith through missionary activity.

israelites.s: The Israelites were an ancient Semitic people of the Levant, ancestors of the Jewish people, who formed the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. The Assyrian Empire conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and deported much of its population.

istami.s: Istämi was a Turkic ruler who governed the western part of the Gokturk realm in the sixth century CE, brother of Bumin, founder of the khaganate. Under Muqan Qaghan he drove westward past the Caspian into former Hephthalite territory.

istanbul.s: Istanbul is the city on the Bosporus formerly known as Constantinople, taken by the Ottomans in 1453. It became the capital of the Ottoman Empire and one of the largest and most cosmopolitan cities of the world.

italian-city-states.s: The Italian city-states were self-governing cities of medieval and Renaissance Italy, such as Venice, Genoa, Pisa and Florence. Venice and Genoa in particular built maritime trading networks across the Mediterranean.

italian-east-africa.s: Italian East Africa was the colonial federation created by Italy in 1936 after the conquest of Ethiopia, combining Ethiopia with Eritrea and Italian Somaliland. It was governed from Addis Ababa.

italian-empire.s: The Italian Empire was the colonial empire of the Kingdom of Italy, built from the late nineteenth century until the Second World War. It included Eritrea, Somalia, Libya and, from 1936, Ethiopia.

italian-somaliland.s: Italian Somaliland was an Italian colony on the Indian Ocean coast of the Horn of Africa, in present-day Somalia. It was one of the earliest acquisitions of the Italian Empire and later part of Italian East Africa.

italian-unification.s: Italian unification, or the Risorgimento, was the political process that united the states of the Italian peninsula into a single kingdom, proclaimed in 1861. Leading figures included Cavour, Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel II.

italian-wars.s: The Italian Wars were a series of conflicts between 1494 and 1559 fought mainly between France and Spain, along with other powers, for control of Italy. Spain emerged dominant, gaining control of Naples and Milan.

italo-turkish-war.s: The Italo-Turkish War of 1911–1912 was fought between Italy and the Ottoman Empire. Italy seized Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, which became the colony of Libya, along with the Dodecanese islands.

italy.s: Italy is a peninsula and country in southern Europe, the homeland of the Roman Empire. It was a battleground for Carthage under Hannibal, and later contested by the Byzantine, Carolingian, Holy Roman and Spanish empires.

itzcoatl.s: Itzcoatl was the Mexica ruler who formed the alliance with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco and the city-state of Tlacopan against the Tepanec power of Azcapotzalco. Their victory in 1428 created the Triple Alliance.

ivan-iii.s: Ivan III was Grand Prince of Moscow in the late fifteenth century, often called Ivan the Great. He unified much of north-eastern Russia under Moscow, annexed Novgorod and ended Tatar overlordship after the stand on the Ugra River in 1480.

ivan-iv-of-russia.s: Ivan IV, known as Ivan the Terrible, was the first ruler of Muscovy to be crowned tsar. He conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and fought the long Livonian War in the Baltic.

ivory-trade.s: The ivory trade is the commerce in elephant tusks, prized for carving and luxury goods. African ivory was traded for thousands of years, from the Egyptian New Kingdom, the Kushite Empire and the Aksumite Empire to later states.

iwan.s: An iwan is a vaulted hall or space, walled on three sides and open on one, characteristic of Persian and Islamic architecture. The four-iwan plan, with iwans facing a central courtyard, became standard for mosques and madrasas.

iron-age.s: The Iron Age is the period in which iron replaced bronze as the main metal for tools and weapons, beginning in the eastern Mediterranean and Near East around 1200 BCE and reaching northern Europe several centuries later. Its dates differ by region.

ibn-qasi.s: Ibn Qasi was a Sufi leader of the Algarve who led the Muridin revolt against the Almoravids in 1144, seizing Mértola and Silves and ruling as an independent lord. He first sought Almohad help, then turned against them and allied with Afonso Henriques of Portugal.

ibn-saud.s: Ibn Saud, Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd al-Rahman Al Saud, recaptured Riyadh from the Rashidis in 1902 and rebuilt Saudi power in central Arabia. He took al-Hasa in 1913, destroyed the Rashidi emirate of Jabal Shammar in 1921 and conquered the Hejaz in 1924–1925.

inner-mongolia.s: Inner Mongolia is the southern part of the Mongolian plateau, lying along the north of China, now an autonomous region of the People's Republic of China. Its grasslands were the home of the Donghu, Xianbei and Wuhuan and the base of states such as Dai.

irish-sea.s: The Irish Sea lies between Ireland and Great Britain, joined to the Atlantic by the North Channel and St George's Channel, with the Isle of Man near its centre. Since prehistory it has carried trade, migration and raids between Ireland, Wales, Scotland and northern England.

imad-al-din-zengi.s: Imad al-Din Zengi was a Turkish atabeg who became governor of Mosul in 1127 and Aleppo in 1128, founding the Zengid dynasty. He spent years trying to take Damascus from its Burid rulers, the Begteginid dynasty, and in 1144 captured Edessa, destroying the first of the crusader…

indian-territory.s: Indian Territory was the land west of Arkansas, in present-day Oklahoma, set aside by the United States for Native American nations removed from the east under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. The Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee and Seminole were resettled there and…

ibn-ammar.s: Ibn Ammar was an Andalusi poet from Silves and the friend and vizier of al-Mutamid of Seville. He accompanied al-Mutamid as governor of Silves and in 1078 took Murcia for Seville, but then ruled it in defiance of his master.

idris-ii.s: Idris II was the posthumous son of Idris I, founder of the Idrisid dynasty in Morocco. He took power around 803 and made Fez his capital, settling refugees from Córdoba and Kairouan in its two quarters.

ionian-revolt.s: The Ionian Revolt was a rising of the Greek cities of Ionia and other parts of Asia Minor and Cyprus against Persian rule, from 499 to 493 BCE. Led at first by Aristagoras of Miletus and supported briefly by Athens and Eretria, it ended after the Persian naval victory at Lade…

isaac-komnenos-of-cyprus.s: Isaac Komnenos was a Byzantine aristocrat and great-nephew of Emperor Manuel I who seized Cyprus in 1184 and ruled it as a self-proclaimed emperor. His harsh rule ended when Richard the Lionheart, on his way to the Third Crusade, conquered the island in 1191.

ismail-kamil-pasha.s: Ismail Kamil Pasha was a son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt. In 1820 and 1821 he led the Egyptian army that defeated the Shaigiya and conquered the Funj Sultanate, beginning Turco-Egyptian rule in the Sudan.

isma-il-pasha.s: Isma'il Pasha was a grandson of Muhammad Ali who ruled Egypt from 1863 and received the title khedive from the Ottoman sultan in 1867. He modernised Cairo, expanded railways and education, opened the Suez Canal in 1869 and extended Egyptian rule in Sudan.

irish-war-of-independence.s: The Irish War of Independence was a guerrilla war fought by the Irish Republican Army against British forces in Ireland. It followed Sinn Féin's election victory and the declaration of independence by Dáil Éireann in 1919.

ibn-mardanish.s: Ibn Mardanish, called the Wolf King by Christian writers, ruled Murcia and Valencia in eastern al-Andalus from 1147 until his death. He resisted the Almohads by allying with Castile, Aragon and the Italian maritime cities, paying tribute and employing Christian soldiers, among…

idris-of-libya.s: Idris of Libya, Muhammad Idris al-Senussi, was head of the Senussi order and leader of Cyrenaica. Exiled in Egypt from 1922 during the Italian conquest, he allied with Britain in the Second World War, became emir of Cyrenaica in 1949 and king of the independent United Kingdom…

ikeda-mitsumasa.s: Ikeda Mitsumasa was a daimyo of the early Edo period who received Tottori domain in 1617 and exchanged it for Okayama in Bizen in 1632. A strict Confucian ruler, he reformed his domain's administration, restricted Buddhist temples and promoted learning, and in 1670 founded the…

ioannis-kapodistrias.s: Ioannis Kapodistrias was a Corfiot nobleman who served as a secretary of state of the Septinsular Republic and then as a Russian diplomat and joint foreign minister of Russia from 1816 to 1822. Elected first governor of Greece in 1827, he arrived in 1828 and built a central…

isa-bin-salman-al-khalifa.s: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa was ruler of Bahrain from 1961 until his death. He led the country to independence from British protection in August 1971 and took the title emir.

iskandar-muda.s: Iskandar Muda was sultan of Aceh from 1607 to 1636, the height of its power. He controlled the pepper trade of northern Sumatra, curbed the great merchant-nobles and conquered Aru, Pahang, Kedah and other states on both sides of the Strait of Malacca, carrying off their rulers…

issa-clan.s: The Issa are a Somali clan of the Dir family, living in Djibouti, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and north-western Somalia. In the 1880s French officers such as Léonce Lagarde signed protection treaties with Issa clans, and their coast became part of French Somaliland.

ivan-asen-ii.s: Ivan Asen II, son of Ivan Asen I, was tsar of Bulgaria from 1218 to 1241. In 1230 he defeated and captured Theodore Komnenos Doukas, ruler of Epirus and Thessalonica, at Klokotnitsa, after which Bulgaria stretched from the Adriatic to the Black Sea and Thessalonica's new ruler…

irish-declaration-of-independence.s: The Irish Declaration of Independence was adopted by Dáil Éireann, the assembly of Sinn Féin members elected in 1918, at its first meeting in Dublin on 21 January 1919. It ratified the Irish Republic proclaimed in 1916 and called on English forces to leave.

ian-smith.s: Ian Smith was a Rhodesian Front politician who became prime minister of Southern Rhodesia in 1964. On 11 November 1965 his government issued the Unilateral Declaration of Independence to avoid majority rule, creating the unrecognised state of Rhodesia.

ibak-khan.s: Ibak Khan was a Shaybanid ruler of the Tyumen Khanate in western Siberia, whose people paid tribute in furs. In 1481, after the Great Stand on the Ugra River, he attacked the camp of Ahmad Khan of the Great Horde and killed him.

ibn-hamdin.s: Ibn Hamdin was the qadi of Córdoba, from a leading family of Maliki jurists, who was proclaimed emir by the city's notables in 1144 during the revolts against the Almoravids. He expelled the Almoravid garrison and ruled the Second Taifa of Córdoba, but his rule was short and…

ibn-hud.s: Ibn Hud, Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Hud al-Mutawakkil, claimed descent from the Hudids of Zaragoza and rose against the Almohads in 1228 in the Ricote valley near Murcia. Recognising the Abbasid caliph, he briefly united much of al-Andalus under his rule, but he lost Córdoba to…

ibn-jahhaf.s: Ibn Jahhaf was the qadi of Valencia who in 1092 led a rising that killed al-Qadir, the Castilian client ruler of the city, and appealed to the Almoravids for help. Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, besieged Valencia, which surrendered in June 1094.

ibrahim-khalil-khan.s: Ibrahim Khalil Khan was khan of Karabakh from 1763, ruling from the fortress of Shusha with the poet Molla Panah Vagif as his vizier. He withstood a siege by Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar in 1795.

ibrahim-nasir.s: Ibrahim Nasir was prime minister of the Maldives under the sultanate from 1957. His government suppressed the secessionist United Suvadive Republic in the southern atolls in 1959–1963 and negotiated independence from Britain in 1965.

ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.s: Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt was the eldest son of Muhammad Ali and the chief commander of his armies. He destroyed the Saudi capital Diriyah in 1818, fought in Greece in the 1820s, and conquered Syria in 1831–1833, defeating the Ottoman army at Konya.

ibrahim-tamghach-khan.s: Ibrahim Tamghach Khan, son of Nasr ibn Ali, took Transoxiana when the Kara-Khanid Khanate divided around 1042 and founded the Western Kara-Khanid Khanate with its capital at Samarkand. He built a strong, centralised state, founded a hospital and a madrasa in Samarkand, and was…

ibrahima-sori.s: Ibrahima Sori, called Mawdo, 'the Great', was a Fulbe military leader of Futa Jallon in present-day Guinea. After the death of the scholar Karamokho Alfa he led the jihad to final victory over the Jallonke and their allies and became almamy.

idi-amin.s: Idi Amin was a Ugandan army officer who seized power from Milton Obote in 1971. He expelled Uganda's Asian community in 1972, and his regime killed tens of thousands of people.

idris-i-of-morocco.s: Idris I was a descendant of the Prophet through Hasan who fled to the Maghreb after a failed Alid revolt against the Abbasids in 786. Welcomed by the Awraba Berbers at Walila, he founded the Idrisid dynasty in 789, conquered much of northern Morocco and founded a town on the…

idris-i-al-mutayyad.s: Idris I al-Muta'ayyad was a member of the Hammudid dynasty, Arab descendants of the Idrisids who claimed the caliphate in al-Andalus after the collapse of Umayyad Córdoba. He succeeded his brother Yahya ibn Ali al-Mutali as ruler of Málaga, the Hammudid base, in 1035, and also…

ii-naosuke.s: Ii Naosuke was lord of the Hikone domain and, from 1858, great elder (tairō) of the Tokugawa shogunate. He signed the Harris Treaty opening Japan to Western trade without imperial approval and purged his opponents in the Ansei Purge, including Tokugawa Nariaki of Mito.

imre-nagy.s: Imre Nagy was a Hungarian communist who as prime minister from 1953 to 1955 eased Stalinist repression before being ousted. During the revolution of October 1956 he returned to power, accepted a multi-party system and declared Hungary's neutrality and withdrawal from the…

international-court-of-justice.s: The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, set up in 1945 and sitting in The Hague. It settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions.

isa-khan.s: Isa Khan was the leader of the Baro-Bhuyans, the landholders of eastern Bengal who resisted Mughal conquest after the fall of the Karrani sultanate in 1576. Ruling from Sonargaon and Katrabo, he relied on river fleets in the delta and defeated a Mughal force in 1584.

isabella-ii-of-spain.s: Isabella II of Spain became queen as an infant in 1833, and her succession set off the Carlist Wars. Her reign was marked by political instability, military coups and scandal at court.

isabella-of-angouleme.s: Isabella of Angoulême, heiress of the county of Angoulême, married King John of England in 1200, which provoked the Lusignans and helped bring on the loss of Normandy. After John's death she returned to France and married Hugh X of Lusignan, count of La Marche, joining his…

islam-karimov.s: Islam Karimov was first secretary of the Communist Party of the Uzbek SSR from 1989 and declared Uzbekistan's independence on 31 August 1991. Elected president that December, he ruled Uzbekistan as an authoritarian leader until his death in 2016, suppressing opposition and…

ismail-bey-of-candar.s: Ismail Bey was the last independent ruler of the Candarid beylik of Kastamonu and Sinop in northern Anatolia. In 1461 Mehmed II, marching against the Empire of Trebizond, took Sinop from him, ending the beylik.

ismail-bey-of-the-nogai-horde.n: Ismail Bey of the Nogai Horde
ismail-bey-of-the-nogai-horde.s: Ismail Bey was a ruler of the Nogai Horde, the nomadic confederation of the Volga steppe. In the 1550s he sided with Ivan IV of Russia during the Russian conquest of the Kazan and Astrakhan khanates, killing his brother Yusuf Bey and taking power.

ismail-qemali.s: Ismail Qemali was an Albanian statesman from Vlorë who had served as an Ottoman official and liberal deputy. On 28 November 1912, during the First Balkan War, he declared Albania's independence at Vlorë and headed its provisional government.

ivan-andreyevich-of-mozhaysk.s: Ivan Andreyevich was prince of Mozhaysk, an appanage of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. In the Muscovite civil war he joined Dmitry Shemyaka, and in 1446 he helped seize Grand Prince Vasily II at the Trinity Monastery, after which Vasily was blinded.

ivar-of-limerick.s: Ivar of Limerick was the Norse king of Limerick in the later 10th century. He allied with Irish kings of Munster against the rising Dál Cais, but Mathgamain and Brian Boru defeated the Norse at Sulcoit in 967 and sacked Limerick.

ilghazi.s: Ilghazi was a Turkmen emir of the Artuqid dynasty who ruled Mardin and took over Aleppo in 1117–1118. In 1119 he destroyed the army of the Principality of Antioch at the Battle of Ager Sanguinis.

imre-szapolyai.s: Imre Szapolyai was a Hungarian magnate and a leading commander under King Matthias Corvinus. He served as ban of Jajce and of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia, defending the southern frontier against the Ottomans, and later as palatine of Hungary.

iwaz-khalji.s: Iwaz Khalji, who ruled Bengal as Sultan Ghiyath al-Din from about 1212 to 1227, was the most capable ruler of the Khalji dynasty of Bengal. He built roads and embankments, created a river fleet and struck coins in his own name.

ibrahim-ibn-hamushk.s: Ibrahim ibn Hamushk was a commander in al-Andalus who seized Jaén and the castles of the Sierra de Segura during the collapse of Almoravid rule after 1145. He was father-in-law and ally of Muhammad ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King of Murcia, against the Almohads, though he later…

ibn-mahfuz.s: Ibn Mahfuz, Shuayb ibn Muhammad ibn Mahfuz, made himself independent ruler of Niebla and its district around 1234 as Ibn Hud's power faded. He became a tributary of Castile and ruled the last independent Muslim state in western al-Andalus until Alfonso X besieged and took…

ibn-maymun.s: Ibn Maymun was the leading figure of a family of admirals who had commanded the Almoravid fleet at Almería, the chief port and naval base of al-Andalus. When Almería rose against the Almoravids in 1145 he became one of its local rulers, during a brief independence ended when…

ibn-rashiq.s: Ibn Rashiq was an officer of the poet-vizier Ibn Ammar who took over the rule of Murcia in the early 1080s, defying al-Mutamid of Seville. His dealings with the Castilian garrison at Aledo made him unpopular, and after the Almoravid siege of Aledo in 1088 Yusuf ibn Tashfin…

ibn-rusta.s: Ibn Rusta was a Persian geographer of the early 10th century, probably from Isfahan, author of the Book of Precious Records. His work includes some of the earliest descriptions of the peoples of eastern Europe and the Caucasus, among them the Rus', the Khazars, the Magyars and…

ibn-tayfur.s: Ibn Tayfur was a local leader who made Mértola, an old river port on the Guadiana in southern Portugal, independent around 1033. His small taifa lasted little more than a decade before it was absorbed by the Aftasid Taifa of Badajoz or the Abbadids of Seville.

ibrahim-adeer.s: Ibrahim Adeer was the founder of the Gobroon dynasty of the Geledi Sultanate in southern Somalia. After the fall of the Ajuran Sultanate he overthrew local rivals around Afgooye on the Shabelle river.

ibrahim-adil-shah-ii.s: Ibrahim Adil Shah II was Sultan of Bijapur from 1580 to 1627, under whom the Deccan sultanate reached its greatest extent and prosperity. A musician and poet, he wrote the Kitab-i-Nauras, songs in Dakhni, and was tolerant of Hindus and different Muslim sects.

ibrahim-dabo.s: Ibrahim Dabo was Emir of Kano from 1819 to 1846, the second ruler of the emirate created by the Fulani jihad within the Sokoto Caliphate. He suppressed revolts, strengthened the emirate's administration and promoted trade and learning.

ibrahim-heski.s: Ibrahim Heski was a Kurdish tribal leader of the Jalali in the Mount Ararat region. During the Ararat rebellion against the Turkish Republic he served as civil governor of the Republic of Ararat, proclaimed in 1927, with Ihsan Nuri Pasha as military commander.

ibrahim-ibn-hajjaj.s: Ibrahim ibn Hajjaj was an Arab noble of Seville who made the city an autonomous lordship during the fitna that shook the Emirate of Córdoba in the late 9th century. Nominally loyal to the emir, he ruled as an independent prince, kept a court of poets and scholars, and made…

ibrahim-ii-of-karaman.s: Ibrahim II was ruler of the Karamanid beylik in south-central Anatolia from 1424 to 1464. He fought the Ottomans repeatedly, often allied with crusaders and other Turkish rivals, and built mosques and madrasas in Karaman and Konya.

ibrahim-ii-of-ifriqiya.s: Ibrahim II was the Aghlabid emir of Ifriqiya from 875 to 902. He built the palace city of Raqqada near Kairouan and continued the conquest of Sicily, taking Syracuse in 878.

ibrahim-khan-of-lar.s: Ibrahim Khan was the last ruler of the Kingdom of Lar, a Sunni principality in southern Persia controlling trade routes to the Persian Gulf. In 1601 to 1602 the Safavid general Allahverdi Khan conquered Lar for Shah Abbas I and deposed him, and Laristan became a Safavid province.

ibrahim-nagwamatse.s: Ibrahim Nagwamatse was Emir of Kontagora from 1880, son of the emirate's founder Umaru Nagwamatse. Under him the slave raiding on which Kontagora lived reached its peak, depopulating much of the region.

ibrahim-pasha-baban.s: Ibrahim Pasha Baban was a ruler of the Baban emirate, a Kurdish principality in the mountains of Shahrizor. In 1784 he founded the city of Sulaymaniyah as his new capital, naming it after Büyük Süleyman Pasha, the Mamluk governor of Baghdad.

ibrahim-shah-sharqi.s: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi was Sultan of Jaunpur from 1402 to 1440, the greatest ruler of the Sharqi dynasty. He welcomed scholars fleeing from Delhi, making Jaunpur known as the Shiraz of India, and built the Atala Mosque in a distinctive style with massive gateways.

ibrahim-zaki.s: Ibrahim Zaki was a Fulani scholar and commander who took up the jihad of Usman dan Fodio on the western frontier of the Kanem-Bornu Empire. In 1808 he joined other Fulani leaders in capturing the Bornu capital, Birni Ngazargamu.

ide-anak-agung-gde-agung.s: Ide Anak Agung Gde Agung was a prince of the Gianyar royal house in Bali who became an Indonesian statesman and historian. He was prime minister of the State of East Indonesia in the federal period and later Indonesia's foreign minister from 1955 to 1956.

ignacy-krasicki.s: Ignacy Krasicki was a Polish poet and churchman, the leading writer of the Polish Enlightenment, known for his fables, satires and the first Polish novel. He became Prince-Bishop of Warmia in 1766, but the First Partition of Poland in 1772 gave Warmia to Prussia.

ignazio-bonafous.s: Ignazio Bonafous was a Piedmontese Jacobin from Alba. In April 1796, as Napoleon's army drove back the troops of the Kingdom of Sardinia, he and Giovanni Antonio Ranza proclaimed the Republic of Alba, hoping for French support for a revolution in Piedmont.

ihsan-nuri-pasha.s: Ihsan Nuri Pasha was a Kurdish former Ottoman and Turkish army officer who became military commander of the Ararat rebellion. Under the Xoybûn organisation he led the rebels of the Republic of Ararat from 1927 until Turkish forces crushed the revolt in 1930.

ii-naomasa.s: Ii Naomasa was one of the four great generals of Tokugawa Ieyasu, commander of the red-armoured troops of the Ii. Wounded at Sekigahara in 1600, he received the former lands of Ishida Mitsunari at Sawayama.

ikeda-terumasa.s: Ikeda Terumasa was a daimyo and son-in-law of Tokugawa Ieyasu who fought for him at Sekigahara. Rewarded with Harima province and 520,000 koku, he rebuilt Himeji Castle between 1601 and 1609 into the great white keep that survives today, a World Heritage Site.

ikeda-tsunamasa.s: Ikeda Tsunamasa was daimyo of Okayama from 1672, son of the Confucian reformer Ikeda Mitsumasa. He carried on his father's land reclamation and completed the Kōrakuen garden in 1700, now one of the three great gardens of Japan.

ikeda-yoshinori.s: Ikeda Yoshinori was the last daimyo of the Tottori domain, a son of Tokugawa Nariaki of Mito and brother of the last shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu. Despite these ties he sided with the imperial forces in the Boshin War of 1868.

ikhtiyaruddin-ghazi-shah.s: Ikhtiyaruddin Ghazi Shah was the second and last independent sultan of Sonargaon in eastern Bengal, succeeding his father Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah around 1349. In 1352 Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah of Lakhnauti conquered Sonargaon, uniting all of Bengal under the Bengal Sultanate.

ikoma-chikamasa.s: Ikoma Chikamasa was a samurai who served Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, from whom he received Sanuki province in 1587. In 1588 he began Takamatsu castle, a sea castle with moats fed by seawater.

ilham-aliyev.s: Ilham Aliyev is the president of Azerbaijan, succeeding his father Heydar Aliyev in 2003. His government has used oil and gas revenue to build up the state and armed forces while suppressing opposition.

ilinden-preobrazhenie-uprising.s: The Ilinden–Preobrazhenie Uprising was a revolt against Ottoman rule organised by the Internal Macedonian-Adrianople Revolutionary Organisation in August 1903. It began on Saint Elijah's Day in Macedonia, where rebels held Kruševo for ten days, and spread to the Strandzha…

illig-qaghan.s: Illig Qaghan was the last ruler of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, reigning from 620. He raided Tang China repeatedly and reached the Wei River near Chang'an in 626.

illinois-country.s: The Illinois Country was the French name for the middle Mississippi valley, in present-day Illinois and Missouri. From the late 17th century French settlers founded villages such as Kaskaskia and Cahokia there, and from 1717 it was governed as part of Louisiana, supplying…

ilona-zrinyi.s: Ilona Zrínyi was a Croatian-Hungarian noblewoman, widow of Francis I Rákóczi and mother of Francis II Rákóczi. In 1682 she married the Kuruc leader Imre Thököly.

ilyas-bey-of-menteshe.s: Ilyas Bey was ruler of the Turkish beylik of Menteshe in south-western Anatolia, restored to his lands by Timur after the Battle of Ankara in 1402. In 1404 he built the İlyas Bey Mosque at Balat beside the ruins of Miletus.

imad-al-dawla.s: Imad al-Dawla, Ali ibn Buya, was the eldest of the three Daylamite brothers who founded the Buyid dynasty. He took Fars and made Shiraz his base in 934, while his brothers took Ray and Baghdad.

imad-al-din-abu-bakr.s: Imad al-Din Abu Bakr was a member of the Artuqid dynasty who established a separate Artuqid line at Harput in 1185, breaking away from the Artuqids of Hasankeyf. His small emirate ruled the Harput region until it was annexed by the Sultanate of Rum in 1234.

imad-shahi-dynasty.s: The Imad Shahi dynasty ruled the Berar Sultanate, the smallest of the Deccan sultanates, from Ellichpur in central India. It was founded around 1490 by Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk, a Bahmani governor, as the Bahmani Sultanate broke up.

imagawa-yoshimoto.s: Imagawa Yoshimoto was a Sengoku daimyo who ruled Suruga, Tōtōmi and Mikawa from Sunpu, one of the most powerful lords of eastern Japan. Marching towards Kyoto in 1560, he was killed in a surprise attack by Oda Nobunaga's much smaller force at Okehazama.

imayavaramban-nedunceralatan.s: Imayavaramban Nedunceralatan was a Chera king of the Sangam period in present-day Kerala and western Tamil Nadu. His title means one who had the Himalaya as his boundary.

imperial-airways.s: Imperial Airways was the British long-range airline formed in 1924 to link the British Empire by air. Its routes to India, Africa and Australia needed landing grounds across the Middle East, and in 1932 it opened a rest house and airfield at Sharjah on the Gulf.

imre-thokoly.s: Imre Thököly was a Hungarian Lutheran noble who led the Kuruc rebellion against Habsburg rule from 1678. With Ottoman backing he ruled the Principality of Upper Hungary from 1682 and married Ilona Zrínyi.

imru-al-qays-ibn-amr.s: Imru al-Qays ibn Amr was an Arab king of the early 4th century, usually counted as an early Lakhmid ruler of al-Hira. His epitaph, the Namara inscription of 328 found in southern Syria, calls him king of all the Arabs and is one of the earliest texts in the Arabic language.

imru-al-qais.s: Imru' al-Qais was a pre-Islamic Arab poet, a prince of the royal house of Kinda, often regarded as the greatest poet of the Jahiliyya. His ode is one of the Mu'allaqat, the most famous collection of early Arabic poetry.

inanc-bey.s: Inanç Bey was a Turkish frontier lord in western Anatolia who gave his name to the Inançid beylik, centred on Ladik near ancient Laodicea, modern Denizli. The beylik lay on the trade road through the Meander valley and was known for gold-embroidered cotton textiles described…

inanch-bilge-khan.s: Inanch Bilge Khan was ruler of the Naiman, a powerful Turkic-Mongol confederation of western Mongolia in the late 12th century. After his death the khanate split between his rival sons Tayang Khan and Buyruk Khan, whose division helped Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, defeat…

independent-social-democratic-party-of-g.n: Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany
independent-social-democratic-party-of-g.s: The Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany (USPD) was formed in 1917 by socialists who broke with the Social Democrats over support for the First World War. It played a leading role in the revolution of 1918–1919 and in council governments such as that of Bremen.

indian-national-army.s: The Indian National Army was a force raised with Japanese support, largely from Indian prisoners of war captured in Malaya and Singapore, to fight British rule in India. Revived under Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943, it served as the army of Azad Hind and fought in the Imphal and…

indochinese-communist-party.s: The Indochinese Communist Party was the communist party founded by Ho Chi Minh in Hong Kong in 1930, merging rival Vietnamese communist groups. Banned and repressed in French Indochina, it created the Viet Minh front in 1941, which seized power in the August Revolution of 1945…

ine-of-wessex.s: Ine of Wessex was king of the West Saxons from 688 to 726, one of the strongest Anglo-Saxon rulers before Alfred. He issued an important law code, founded or endowed churches including Glastonbury, and pushed West Saxon power westward into Somerset and Devon, fighting King…

ingrian-finns.s: The Ingrian Finns are the Lutheran Finnish-speaking population of Ingria, around the Gulf of Finland and modern St Petersburg. They descend mainly from settlers from Savonia and the Karelian Isthmus who moved in under Swedish rule in the 17th century, replacing Orthodox…

inigo-arista.s: Íñigo Arista was the first king of Pamplona, the kingdom later known as Navarre. A Basque leader, he took power around 824 after the Basques defeated a Frankish army at the second Battle of Roncevaux, ending Carolingian control.

inigo-lopez-ezquerra.s: Íñigo López Ezquerra was the first recorded lord or count of Biscay, appearing in documents from about 1040 as a vassal of the kings of Navarre. He founded the line later known as the López de Haro, which held the lordship of Biscay for more than three centuries.

intef-ii.s: Intef II, also called Wahankh, was a king of the Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt who ruled from Thebes for about fifty years during the First Intermediate Period. He claimed the title of king of Upper and Lower Egypt, fought the rival Herakleopolitan kings for Thinis and Abydos, and…

internal-macedonian-revolutionary-organi.s: The Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization was a secret revolutionary society founded in Thessaloniki in 1893 to win autonomy for Macedonia and the Adrianople region from Ottoman rule. In 1903 it launched the Ilinden Uprising in Macedonia, during which rebels…

ioannis-malachias.s: Ioannis Malachias was a Greek doctor who led the uprising on the Aegean island of Icaria in July 1912, during the Italo-Turkish War. The islanders forced the small Ottoman garrison to surrender and proclaimed the Free State of Icaria, with Malachias as its leading figure.

ioannis-rallis.s: Ioannis Rallis was a Greek politician who served as the third and last collaborationist prime minister of Greece under the Axis occupation, from 1943 to 1944. He created the Security Battalions, armed units that fought alongside the Germans against the communist-led resistance…

ion-iliescu.s: Ion Iliescu was a Romanian politician who led the National Salvation Front after the revolution of December 1989 overthrew Nicolae Ceaușescu. A former communist official, he was elected president in 1990 and again in 1992 and 2000.

ion-inculet.s: Ion Inculeț was a Bessarabian physicist and politician who presided over the Sfatul Țării, the council that proclaimed the Moldavian Democratic Republic in December 1917. As its president he oversaw the council's vote of April 1918 for union with Romania.

iron-crown-of-lombardy.s: The Iron Crown of Lombardy is a medieval crown of gold and jewels, kept in the cathedral of Monza, whose inner band was said to be made from a nail of the True Cross. It was used to crown kings of Italy, including several Holy Roman Emperors in their Italian kingship.

iron-gates.s: The Iron Gates are the gorge of the Danube where it cuts through the Carpathian and Balkan mountains, today forming part of the border between Serbia and Romania. For centuries a dangerous stretch for navigation and a strategic crossing point, the area was guarded by Roman and…

iron-gates-algeria.s: The Iron Gates of Algeria, known in French as the Portes de Fer, are a narrow pass through the Biban mountains between Algiers and Constantine. The defile carried the main route between the coast and eastern Algeria, and control of it gave the Kabyle rulers of the Kalâa of the…

isaac-the-armenian.s: Isaac the Armenian was the Byzantine exarch of Ravenna from 625 to 643, governing imperial Italy on behalf of the emperor. An Armenian noble, he dealt with the Lombard kingdom and with the papacy, and in 640 his troops plundered the Lateran treasury in Rome.

isaac-of-theodoro.s: Isaac of Theodoro was prince of the small Orthodox principality of Theodoro, centred on Mangup in the mountains of southern Crimea, in the 1460s and early 1470s. Ruling between the Genoese colonies of the coast and the Crimean Khanate, he sought accommodation with the Ottomans.

isabella-jagiellon.s: Isabella Jagiellon was a Polish princess, daughter of Sigismund I the Old, who married John Zápolya, king of Hungary, in 1539. After his death in 1540 she governed the eastern Hungarian kingdom as regent for their infant son John Sigismund, with Bishop George Martinuzzi.

isaias-afwerki.s: Isaias Afwerki is an Eritrean politician who led the Eritrean People's Liberation Front in the war of independence against Ethiopia and has been president of Eritrea since independence in 1993. His People's Front for Democracy and Justice is the only legal party, the…

isatay-taimanuly.s: Isatay Taimanuly was a Kazakh batyr and elder of the Bukey Horde who led a revolt from 1836 to 1838 against Jangir Khan and the Russian-backed elite. Together with the poet Makhambet Otemisuly he protested the khan's land grants and heavy exactions on ordinary herders.

ishak-bey-of-saruhan.s: Ishak Bey was ruler of the Turkish beylik of Saruhan in western Anatolia, with its capital at Manisa, in the second half of the 14th century. He was the son of the dynasty's founder Saruhan Bey.

ishaq-ibn-muhammad-of-carmona.s: Ishaq ibn Muhammad was a ruler of the taifa of Carmona in al-Andalus in the mid-11th century, a member of the Berber Birzalid family who had taken the town after the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba. Pressed by the expanding Abbadid rulers of Seville, the Birzalids kept a…

ishaq-ibn-ghaniya.s: Ishaq ibn Muhammad ibn Ghaniya was emir of Majorca from about 1155 to 1183, the leading ruler of the Banu Ghaniya, a branch of the Almoravid family that kept the Balearic Islands after the Almoravid Empire collapsed. Under him Majorca prospered from trade and corsair raids,…

isidoro-midel.s: Isidoro Midel was a Filipino revolutionary leader in Zamboanga during the Philippine Revolution. After Vicente Alvarez was ousted amid factional rivalries, Midel headed the government of the Republic of Zamboanga in 1899 and negotiated with the Americans.

ismail-abd-al-nabi.s: Ismail Abd al-Nabi was a Masalit holy man who built up authority among the Masalit people on the western fringe of the Darfur Sultanate in the 1870s, as Darfur fell to Zubayr Pasha and Egypt. His family founded the independent Sultanate of Dar Masalit around 1874, which…

ismail-al-zafir.s: Ismail al-Zafir, of the Berber family of the Banu Dhi al-Nun, was the first ruler of the dynasty in the taifa of Toledo. Formerly lords of Uclés and Huete, the family was invited by Toledo's notables after the city threw off caliphal rule, and Ismail established the dynasty…

ismail-ibn-ahmad.s: Isma'il ibn Ahmad, known as Ismail Samani, was the Samanid emir who made his family the rulers of Transoxiana and Khurasan. Governor of Bukhara under his brother Nasr, he defeated the Saffarid Amr ibn al-Layth in 900 and ruled from Bukhara as governor for the Abbasid caliph,…

ismail-khan-of-shaki.s: Ismail Khan was the last khan of Shaki, a khanate in the north of present-day Azerbaijan, which had accepted Russian protection in 1805. Installed under Russian oversight, he ruled until his death in 1819, after which the Russian Empire abolished the khanate and turned it into…

ismail-omar-guelleh.s: Ismail Omar Guelleh is a Djiboutian politician who has been president of Djibouti since 1999, succeeding his uncle Hassan Gouled Aptidon. A former head of the security services, he has won repeated elections dominated by his ruling coalition.

istvan-tisza.s: István Tisza was a Hungarian statesman who served as prime minister of Hungary in 1903–1905 and 1913–1917. Son of the prime minister Kálmán Tisza, he was a determined defender of the Dualist settlement with Austria and of the political dominance of the Hungarian gentry, and…

itchan-kala.s: Itchan Kala is the walled inner town of Khiva in Uzbekistan, the historic core of the city and the seat of the khans of Khiva. Its mud-brick walls enclose palaces, mosques, madrasas and minarets, most of them built in the 18th and 19th centuries under the Qungrat dynasty,…

itzamnaaj-kawiil.s: Itzamnaaj K'awiil was the second known ruler of the Maya city of Dos Pilas in Guatemala, reigning from 698 to 726. Son of the dynasty's founder B'ajlaj Chan K'awiil, he continued his father's alliance with Calakmul and expanded Dos Pilas power across the Petexbatún region.

ivan-crnojevic.s: Ivan Crnojević was lord of Zeta, the forerunner of Montenegro, from 1465 to 1490. Caught between Venice and the Ottoman Empire, he fought the Ottomans in alliance with Venice and lost his lands for a time.

ivan-dmitrievich-of-pereslavl.s: Ivan Dmitrievich was the last prince of Pereslavl-Zalessky, a son of Grand Prince Dmitry of Vladimir and grandson of Alexander Nevsky. He died childless in 1302 and bequeathed his principality to his uncle Daniel of Moscow.

ivan-ivanovich-of-ryazan.s: Ivan Ivanovich was the last grand prince of Ryazan, ruling from 1500. Seeking to free his principality from the growing control of Moscow, he was suspected of negotiating with the Crimean Khanate, and in 1520 or 1521 Grand Prince Vasily III summoned and imprisoned him.

ivan-paskevich.s: Ivan Paskevich was a Russian field marshal who won the wars against Persia in 1826–1828 and the Ottoman Empire in 1828–1829. He captured Erivan in 1827, for which he was named Count of Erivan, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay gave the khanate to Russia.

ivan-sratsimir.s: Ivan Sratsimir was tsar of Bulgaria at Vidin from 1356 to 1396. The eldest son of Tsar Ivan Alexander, he was passed over as heir in favour of his half-brother Ivan Shishman and given the north-western region around Vidin, where he ruled as a separate and rival tsar.

ivan-subasic.s: Ivan Šubašić was a Croatian politician of the Croatian Peasant Party who served as ban of the autonomous Banovina of Croatia from 1939 to 1941. After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia he went into exile, and in 1944 became prime minister of the Yugoslav government-in-exile,…

ivan-vladimirovich-of-pronsk.s: Ivan Vladimirovich was prince of Pronsk, a principality in the Ryazan lands south-east of Moscow. Like other princes of Pronsk he contested the senior throne of Ryazan with his cousins, and in 1408, with Tatar support from the Golden Horde, he briefly drove out the grand…

ivan-vsevolodovich-of-starodub.s: Ivan Vsevolodovich was the youngest son of Grand Prince Vsevolod the Big Nest of Vladimir and the first prince of Starodub on the Klyazma. He is usually said to have received the town from his brother Yaroslav in 1238, after the Mongol invasion.

ivory-coast.s: Ivory Coast, officially Côte d'Ivoire, is a country on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa. It became a French colony in 1893 and part of French West Africa, growing into the federation's leading producer of coffee and cocoa, with labour drawn partly from Upper Volta.

izz-al-din-masud-i.s: Izz al-Din Mas'ud I was the Zengid atabeg of Mosul from 1180 to 1193, a nephew of Nur al-Din. He competed with Saladin for the leadership of the Zengid lands in Syria and northern Mesopotamia and withstood Saladin's sieges of Mosul.

izz-al-din-saltuk-ii.s: Izz al-Din Saltuk II was ruler of the Saltukids, a Turkish dynasty based at Erzurum in eastern Anatolia, in the mid-12th century. His lands bordered the Kingdom of Georgia, and in the 1150s he was defeated and captured by the Georgians, then ransomed.

izz-al-din-shir.s: Izz al-Din Shir was a Kurdish emir of Hakkari in the late 14th century, ruling from Julamerk in the mountains of south-eastern Anatolia. When Timur's armies came through the region he submitted to the conqueror and was allowed to keep his lands.

ismail-khan-qashqai.s: Ismail Khan Qashqai, titled Solat al-Dowleh, was ilkhan of the Qashqai tribal confederation in southern Iran. During the First World War he fought the British-led South Persia Rifles.

instructions-of-the-year-xiii.s: The Instructions of the Year XIII were the directions given in April 1813 by José Gervasio Artigas and a congress of the Eastern Province to its deputies at the assembly in Buenos Aires. They called for independence from Spain, a republican government, a federal union of the…

ishvarasena.s: Ishvarasena was an Abhira king who founded a kingdom around Nashik in western India in the 3rd century CE, as the Satavahana dynasty weakened. He is known mainly from a Prakrit inscription in the Buddhist caves at Nashik, dated to the ninth year of his reign, and from coins.

inaros-ii.s: Inaros II was a Libyan prince who led a revolt against Persian rule in Egypt from about 460 BCE. With help from an Athenian fleet he defeated the satrap Achaemenes and besieged the Persians in Memphis.

ibrahim-i-ibn-al-aghlab.s: Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab was an Arab army commander who founded the Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya. In 800 the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid made him hereditary governor of the province in return for an annual tribute, giving his family virtual independence.

itzamna.s: Itzamna was one of the principal gods of the Maya, a creator deity associated with the sky, writing, knowledge and healing, often shown as an old man. At the time of the Spanish conquest he was honoured at Izamal in northern Yucatán, a pilgrimage centre with great pyramids.

izamal.s: Izamal is a town in the Mexican state of Yucatán, built over a large Maya city whose pyramids, among them Kinich Kak Moo, are some of the largest in the peninsula. A pilgrimage centre of the god Itzamna, it belonged to the Chel province after the fall of Mayapan.

ibn-sulaym-al-aswani.s: Ibn Sulaym al-Aswani was a 10th-century Egyptian official and writer, sent around 969 by the Fatimid commander Jawhar as envoy to the Christian king of Makuria. His History of Nubia, now lost but quoted by later authors such as al-Maqrizi, is the main surviving description of…

indigenous-peoples-of-california.s: The Indigenous peoples of California include more than a hundred distinct groups, such as the Chumash, Tongva, Ohlone, Miwok and Pomo, whose ancestors lived there for thousands of years. Under Spanish rule from 1769 many were gathered into missions, where disease and forced…

izumo-province.s: Izumo Province was an old province of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast, in the east of modern Shimane Prefecture. It is the setting of many myths in the Kojiki and home to the Izumo Grand Shrine, one of Japan's oldest Shinto sanctuaries.

indravarma.s: Indravarma was a ruler of the Apracharaja dynasty of Bajaur in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent around the turn of the era. He is known from coins and from a Buddhist reliquary he dedicated, the Bajaur casket.

ikskile.s: Ikšķile, German Üxküll, is a town on the Daugava river in Latvia, south-east of Riga. There the missionary Meinhard built a church and one of the first stone castles in the Baltic region in the 1180s.

ibibio-people.s: The Ibibio are a people of south-eastern Nigeria, living mainly in Akwa Ibom State between the Cross River and the coast. Organised in village groups rather than large kingdoms, they are known for the Ekpo masking society and for wood carving, and they traded with the Aro and…

ibini-ukpabi.s: Ibini Ukpabi was an oracle shrine at Arochukwu in south-eastern Nigeria, known to Europeans as the Long Juju. Consulted by people from across Igboland and beyond to settle disputes, it gave the Aro great authority, and many of those it condemned were sold into slavery.

ismail-al-jazari.s: Ismail al-Jazari was an engineer and inventor who served the Artuqid rulers of Diyarbakır in upper Mesopotamia for about 25 years. Around 1206 he completed his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, describing water clocks, automata, pumps and other machines with…

ichijodani.s: Ichijōdani is a narrow valley near Fukui in Japan, where the Asakura clan built their castle and town in the late 15th century. Under five generations of Asakura rulers it became a prosperous cultural centre that welcomed refugee courtiers and scholars from Kyoto.

ikshvaku.s: Ikshvaku is a legendary king of ancient India, son of Manu, regarded as the founder of the Solar dynasty that ruled Kosala from Ayodhya. Rama, hero of the Ramayana, belonged to his line, and the Buddha's Shakya clan and many later royal houses claimed descent from him.

imperial-asiatic-company-of-trieste.s: The Imperial Asiatic Company of Trieste was an Austrian trading company founded in 1775 on the initiative of William Bolts, a former servant of the British East India Company. Sailing under the Habsburg flag, it set up posts at Delagoa Bay in south-east Africa and on the…

imam-shamil.s: Imam Shamil was an Avar political and religious leader who led the resistance of the peoples of Dagestan and Chechnya against the Russian Empire. Imam of the Caucasian Imamate from 1834, he built a centralised state ruled by sharia law and fought for a quarter of a century.

inshushinak.s: Inshushinak was the patron god of Susa in ancient Elam, whose name means 'lord of Susa' in Sumerian. A god of oaths and of the dead, he became from the 2nd millennium BCE one of the chief gods of the Elamite pantheon, honoured in royal names such as Puzur-Inshushinak and…

isa-bey-mosque.s: The Isa Bey Mosque is a mosque in Selçuk, near ancient Ephesus in western Turkey, built in 1374–1375 for the Aydinid ruler Isa Bey by the architect Ali ibn al-Dimishqi. Its plan, with a large courtyard and a prayer hall set across the long side, reused columns from earlier…

indrayudha.s: Indrayudha was a king of Kannauj in northern India in the late 8th century, the first known ruler of the Ayudha dynasty. The Jain Harivamsha of Jinasena, dated 783, names him as ruling in the north.

ilisu-dam.s: The Ilisu Dam is a large hydroelectric dam on the Tigris in south-eastern Turkey, part of the Southeastern Anatolia Project. Built between 2006 and 2018, it began filling in 2019, and by 2020 its reservoir had submerged most of the ancient town of Hasankeyf and dozens of…

imphal.s: Imphal is the capital of the state of Manipur in north-eastern India, set in a fertile valley ringed by hills. It was the seat of the Meitei kings of Manipur, whose Kangla fort stands at its centre.

indian-wild-ass-sanctuary.s: The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary is a protected area in the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, India, established in 1972. Covering nearly 5,000 square kilometres of salt flats, grassland and seasonal wetland, it is the last refuge of the Indian wild ass, or khur, whose numbers…

ihosy.s: Ihosy is a town in south-central Madagascar, the capital of the Ihorombe region, on the main road between Fianarantsoa and Toliara. It lies on the grassy plateau of the Bara people, cattle herders whose ruling Zafimanely houses established their authority over the region's…

ibn-khallikan.s: Ibn Khallikan was an Arab scholar and judge born in Erbil, who served as chief qadi of Damascus under the Mamluks. He is best known for his biographical dictionary, Wafayat al-A'yan ('Deaths of Eminent Men'), which contains hundreds of carefully dated lives of notable Muslims.

ilyas-shahi-dynasty.s: The Ilyas Shahi dynasty was the first royal house of the united Bengal Sultanate. Its founder, Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, brought all of Bengal under one ruler by 1352 and resisted an invasion by the Delhi Sultanate.

ibrahim-rauza.s: The Ibrahim Rauza is a tomb and mosque complex at Bijapur in Karnataka, India, built for Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II of the Bijapur Sultanate and his queen and completed in the 1620s. Set on a raised platform in a walled garden, its two buildings are admired for their refined…

izmail.s: Izmail is a port town in the Odesa region of Ukraine on the Kiliya branch of the Danube delta. It was an Ottoman fortress commanding the lower Danube, famously stormed by Russian troops under Alexander Suvorov in December 1790, and it changed hands several times between…

iksan.s: Iksan is a city in North Jeolla Province in south-western South Korea. In the Baekje period it was known as Geummajeo and was an important royal centre, with the great Buddhist temple of Mireuksa.

institutional-act-number-five.s: Institutional Act Number Five, known as AI-5, was a decree issued by the Brazilian military government on 13 December 1968 under President Artur da Costa e Silva. It closed Congress, suspended habeas corpus for political crimes, allowed the removal of elected officials and…

institutional-acts.s: The Institutional Acts were seventeen decrees issued by Brazil's military governments between 1964 and 1969, which placed themselves above the constitution. They allowed the regime to purge Congress and the civil service, make presidential and governors' elections indirect,…

isurium-brigantum.s: Isurium Brigantum was a Roman town at Aldborough in North Yorkshire, England, near the River Ure. It grew beside an early Roman fort and became the civitas capital, the administrative centre, of the Brigantes in Roman Britain.

ilocos.s: Ilocos is a region of north-western Luzon in the Philippines, a narrow plain between the Cordillera and the South China Sea, home of the Ilocano people. Its chief town under Spanish rule was Vigan.

indian-independence-act-1947.s: The Indian Independence Act 1947 was an act of the British Parliament that partitioned British India into the two independent dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947. It ended British rule and the British monarch's title of Emperor of India and freed the princely…

international-business-companies-act-bri.n: International Business Companies Act (British Virgin Islands)
international-business-companies-act-bri.s: The International Business Companies Act of 1984 was a law of the British Virgin Islands that allowed the cheap and simple formation of offshore companies with low taxes and few disclosure requirements. It made the territory one of the world's leading centres for company…

idris-katakarmabi.s: Idris Katakarmabi was a mai, or king, of the Kanem-Bornu Empire of the Sayfawa dynasty, who reigned in the early 16th century. He defeated the Bulala, who had driven the Sayfawa out of Kanem, and reoccupied the old capital Njimi, although the dynasty continued to rule from Bornu.

ingapirca.s: Ingapirca is the largest Inca archaeological site in Ecuador, in Cañar province. Built on the Cañari centre of Hatun Cañar after the Inca conquest in the late 15th century, it combines a Cañari burial ground with Inca structures, notably an elliptical temple of finely fitted…

isfendiyar-bey.s: Isfendiyar Bey was a ruler of the Candarid beylik of Kastamonu and Sinop in northern Anatolia, who died in 1440. After the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I took Kastamonu, he regained his family's lands with Timur's backing following the Battle of Ankara in 1402.

incident-at-the-gaoping-tombs.s: The incident at the Gaoping Tombs was the coup of 249 in which Sima Yi seized control of the Cao Wei state. While the regent Cao Shuang escorted the young emperor Cao Fang to the imperial tombs at Gaoping outside Luoyang, Sima Yi took the capital.

ilheus.s: Ilhéus is a port city in southern Bahia, Brazil, founded around 1536 as São Jorge dos Ilhéus, the seat of the hereditary Captaincy of Ilhéus. The colony struggled against indigenous attacks for two centuries.

inconfidencia-mineira.s: The Inconfidência Mineira was a conspiracy for independence from Portugal among officers, priests, poets and landowners of Vila Rica, Minas Gerais, in 1789. Angered by heavy gold taxes and inspired by the American Revolution, they planned a rising for the day of a new tax levy.

imbabura-province.s: Imbabura is a province in the northern highlands of Ecuador, with its capital at Ibarra, named after the Imbabura volcano. It was the homeland of the Caranqui, who resisted the Inca in the late 15th century.
