iruna-veleia.s: Iruña-Veleia is an archaeological site near Vitoria-Gasteiz in Álava, Spain, the remains of the Roman town of Veleia, which grew from a settlement of the Caristii. It flourished on the road from Asturica to Burdigala and was walled in the late Roman period.

isle-of-mull.s: The Isle of Mull is the second-largest island of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland in Argyll, separated from the mainland by the Sound of Mull. In the early Middle Ages it lay within the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata, close to the monastery of Iona off its…

iztaccihuatl.s: Iztaccíhuatl is a dormant volcano in central Mexico, at 5,230 metres the country's third-highest mountain, on the border of the states of Mexico and Puebla. Its name means 'white woman' in Nahuatl, after its snow-covered ridges, which resemble a sleeping woman.

indrapura-champa.s: Indrapura was a capital of Champa in central Vietnam, at Đồng Dương in Quảng Nam province, from the late 9th century. Its great Buddhist monastery, founded by King Indravarman II in 875, was one of the largest in Southeast Asia.

ignacio-bravo.s: Ignacio Bravo was a Mexican general of the Porfirio Díaz era. Sent to Yucatán in 1899 to end the long Caste War, he led the campaign that captured Chan Santa Cruz, the rebel Maya capital, in May 1901, and then held military command in the new federal territory of Quintana Roo…

italicus-cheruscan-king.s: Italicus was a king of the Cherusci in the 1st century CE, a son of Arminius' brother Flavus, who had stayed loyal to Rome. Raised in Rome as a citizen, he was sent by the emperor Claudius in 47 at the request of the Cherusci, whose nobility had been destroyed by internal wars.

iao-valley.s: ʻĪao Valley is a steep, lush valley in the West Maui Mountains above Wailuku, Hawaii, known for the ʻĪao Needle, a rock pinnacle. A sacred burial place of Maui's chiefs, it was the site in 1790 of the Battle of Kepaniwai, in which Kamehameha I, using cannon and foreign…

ibn-bibi.s: Ibn Bibi was a Persian historian of the Sultanate of Rum in the 13th century, a court official who served the Seljuk sultans under their Mongol overlords. His chronicle, al-Awamir al-Alaiya, completed in the 1280s, covers the history of the Seljuks of Anatolia from 1192 to…

ito-hirobumi.s: Itō Hirobumi (1841–1909) was a Japanese statesman from the Chōshū domain and the first prime minister of Japan, serving four times between 1885 and 1901. He led the drafting of the Meiji Constitution of 1889 and founded the Rikken Seiyūkai party in 1900.

iraghticonnor.s: Iraghticonnor, from the Irish Oireacht Uí Chonchúir, "the inheritance of O'Connor", is a barony in north County Kerry, Ireland, lying between the River Feale and the Shannon estuary. It preserves the name of the territory held by the O'Connor Kerry after the Anglo-Norman…

indo-fijians.s: Indo-Fijians are Fijian citizens of Indian descent, most of them descended from about 60,000 indentured labourers brought from India between 1879 and 1916 to work on sugar plantations. By the 1940s they outnumbered indigenous Fijians, but most land remained reserved for Fijian…

iverni.s: The Iverni were a people of southern Ireland recorded in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 CE, with a town called Ivernis in the region of modern Cork or Kerry. Their name is related to Ériu and Hibernia, the old names of Ireland, and scholars link them with the Érainn, the…

ivan-mazepa.s: Ivan Mazepa was hetman of the Cossack Hetmanate from 1687 to 1708 and a generous patron of Orthodox churches, learning and the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy. During the Great Northern War he broke with Peter the Great and joined Charles XII of Sweden in 1708, hoping to free the…

ingelger.s: Ingelger was a 9th-century Frankish noble regarded as the founder of the first dynasty of the counts of Anjou. He held office around Angers and Tours under the Carolingian kings, defending the Loire valley against Viking raids, and his son Fulk the Red became the first…

isabella-of-hainaut.s: Isabella of Hainaut was queen of France as the first wife of Philip II Augustus, whom she married in 1180. A daughter of Baldwin V of Hainaut and niece of Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders, she brought Artois as her dowry, which passed to the French crown.

iserlohn.s: Iserlohn is a town in the Sauerland, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. A town of the County of the Mark from the 13th century, it became known for wire-drawing, needle making and metalwork, and later for brass and bronze goods.

isabena.s: The Isábena is a river of the Pyrenees in the province of Huesca, Aragon, a tributary of the Ésera, which flows into the Cinca. Its valley formed part of the medieval county of Ribagorza, and the village of Roda de Isábena on its banks was the seat of the county's bishopric.

innsbruck.s: Innsbruck is the capital of the Austrian state of Tyrol, on the Inn at the foot of the Nordkette range. Seat of the Tyrolean princes from the 15th century, it was a favoured residence of Emperor Maximilian I, whose Golden Roof and cenotaph in the Court Church are landmarks.

ix-chel.s: Ix Chel is a Maya goddess associated with the moon, childbirth, weaving and medicine. In the Postclassic period pilgrims from across Yucatán, especially women seeking fertility and safe childbirth, travelled to her shrines on the island of Cozumel to consult her oracle.

ischia.s: Ischia is a volcanic island at the northern entrance to the Bay of Naples, in southern Italy. Known to the Greeks as Pithekoussai, it was settled by Euboean traders in the 8th century BCE, one of the earliest Greek settlements in the western Mediterranean, before they founded…

isla-refinery.s: The Isla refinery is an oil refinery on the Schottegat harbour of Willemstad, Curaçao, opened by Royal Dutch Shell in 1918 to process Venezuelan crude oil. It dominated the island's economy for much of the 20th century.

isaac-ii-angelos.s: Isaac II Angelos was Byzantine emperor from 1185 to 1195 and again from 1203 to 1204. Brought to power by a revolt against Andronikos I, he faced the Bulgarian rising that founded the Second Bulgarian Empire and failed to recover Cyprus from Isaac Komnenos.

isabu.s: Isabu, or Kim Isabu, was a general of Silla in the 6th century. In 512 he subdued the island state of Usan (Ulleungdo), reputedly by threatening to release wooden lions, and in 562 he conquered Daegaya, the last of the Gaya states, with the young hwarang Sadaham.

illyricum-roman-province.s: Illyricum was the Roman province on the eastern shore of the Adriatic, formed in stages during the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE as Rome subdued the Illyrian peoples of the coast and hinterland. Julius Caesar governed it with Gaul.

ishtaran.s: Ishtaran was a Mesopotamian god, the patron of the city of Der on the Elamite border. He was regarded as a divine judge and was invoked in border disputes, including a famous one between Lagash and Umma.

ioannina.s: Ioannina is the largest city of Epirus in north-western Greece, on the shore of Lake Pamvotis. A leading city of the medieval Despotate of Epirus, it surrendered to the Ottomans in 1430.

ivanko-of-dobruja.s: Ivanko was the son of Dobrotitsa and the last ruler of the Dobrujan principality on the Black Sea, from about 1386. In 1387 he made treaties with the Ottomans and with Genoa, which held trading posts on the coast.

inzak.s: Inzak, also written Enzak, was the chief god of Dilmun, the Bronze Age civilisation centred on Bahrain. Inscriptions from Bahrain and Failaka name him, and in the Sumerian myth Enki and Ninhursag he is appointed lord of Dilmun.

imperial-conference.s: The Imperial Conferences were periodic meetings in London of the prime ministers of the self-governing parts of the British Empire with the British government, held from 1907 to 1937. Successors to the Colonial Conferences begun in 1887, they discussed defence, trade and the…

igor-of-kiev.s: Igor was the ruler of Kievan Rus' from about 912 to 945, called in the Primary Chronicle the son of Rurik. He led raids on Constantinople in 941 and 944, the first ending in defeat by Greek fire, and concluded a trade treaty with the Byzantine Empire.

ingolstadt.s: Ingolstadt is a city in Upper Bavaria, Germany, on the Danube. From 1392 to 1447 it was the capital of the Duchy of Bavaria-Ingolstadt, and in 1472 Duke Louis IX of Bavaria-Landshut founded Bavaria's first university there, which moved to Landshut and then Munich in the early…

isabeau-of-bavaria.s: Isabeau of Bavaria was Queen of France as the wife of Charles VI, whom she married in 1385. A daughter of Duke Stephen III of Bavaria-Ingolstadt, she took part in government during her husband's bouts of madness, amid the feud between the Armagnacs and the Burgundians.

inflanty-voivodeship.s: The Inflanty Voivodeship was a province of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth formed from the part of Livonia that Poland-Lithuania kept after its 17th-century wars with Sweden, roughly corresponding to Latgale in modern south-eastern Latvia. Its seat was Dyneburg (Daugavpils).

isar.s: The Isar is a river of Tyrol and Bavaria, nearly 300 km long, rising in the Karwendel range of the Alps and flowing north-east past Munich, Freising and Landshut to join the Danube near Deggendorf. Its lower valley formed the heart of Lower Bavaria.

ionian-sea.s: The Ionian Sea is the part of the Mediterranean between southern Italy and western Greece and Albania, linked to the Adriatic in the north by the Strait of Otranto. The Ionian Islands, including Corfu, Ithaca and Zakynthos, lie along its eastern side.

international-force-east-timor.s: The International Force East Timor (INTERFET) was a multinational peacekeeping force led by Australia and authorised by the UN Security Council in September 1999. It deployed after pro-Indonesian militias devastated East Timor following its vote for independence, restored…

ibrium.s: Ibrium was a vizier of Ebla in northern Syria in the 24th century BCE, known from the city's royal archive. He succeeded Arrukum as the leading official of the kingdom and appears in the tablets directing the administration, receiving tribute and leading military campaigns.

isla-mujeres.s: Isla Mujeres is a small island in the Caribbean Sea off the north-east coast of the Yucatán Peninsula, opposite Cancún, in the Mexican state of Quintana Roo. The Maya had a shrine there to the goddess Ixchel, and Spaniards of Francisco Hernández de Córdoba's expedition named…

idumaea.s: Idumaea was the Greek and Roman name for the region of southern Judah, between Hebron and the northern Negev, settled by Edomites after the fall of the Kingdom of Judah. The Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus conquered it in the late 2nd century BCE and made its people adopt Judaism.

igbajo.s: Igbajo is a town in Osun State in south-western Nigeria. Near it lay Kiriji, the fortified war camps where the armies of the Ekiti Parapo confederacy and of Ibadan faced each other for years during the Kiriji War, which began in 1877, until a British-brokered peace treaty of…

igbomina.s: The Igbomina are a Yoruba subgroup living in north-eastern Yorubaland, mostly in Kwara State and parts of Osun State, Nigeria, with towns such as Ila-Orangun and Omu-Aran. In the 19th century they were caught between Ilorin and Ibadan, and some of their towns joined the Ekiti…

ikausu.s: Ikausu was a king of the Philistine city of Ekron in the early 7th century BCE and son of King Padi; his name corresponds to the biblical Achish. He appears in Assyrian records among the western vassals of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal.

ingiloys.s: The Ingiloys are a Georgian-speaking ethnographic group of north-western Azerbaijan, living mainly in the Qakh, Zaqatala and Balakan districts. Descended from the medieval Georgian population of the region of Hereti, many were converted to Islam under Persian and local Muslim…

ilisu.s: Ilisu is a village in the Qakh district of north-western Azerbaijan, in a valley on the southern slopes of the Greater Caucasus. From the early 17th century it was the seat of the sultans of Elisu, who ruled the surrounding Tsakhur and Ingiloy communities until Russia…

ishpabara.s: Ishpabara was a king of Ellipi in the central Zagros in the late 8th century BCE, son of Dalta. When his father died in 708 BCE he fought his brother Nibe for the throne and was installed by Sargon II's Assyrian troops, while Nibe's Elamite allies were driven off.

iamblichus-i-of-emesa.s: Iamblichus I was a ruler of Emesa in Syria, son of Sampsigeramus I, who supported Julius Caesar and other Roman commanders during the civil wars of the 40s and 30s BCE. Accused of treachery before the Battle of Actium, he was executed by Mark Antony in 31 BCE.

ibn-zamrak.s: Ibn Zamrak was a poet and vizier at the Nasrid court of Granada under Muhammad V. A pupil of Ibn al-Khatib, he succeeded his teacher as chief secretary and later turned against him.

ibn-al-khatib.s: Lisan al-Din ibn al-Khatib was a poet, historian, physician and vizier of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada under Yusuf I and Muhammad V. His works include a history of Granada and a treatise arguing that plague spread by contagion.

ibn-al-thumna.s: Ibn al-Thumna was one of the rival Muslim lords who divided Sicily in the 1050s, ruling Syracuse and Catania. Defeated by his rival Ibn al-Hawwas, he went to Count Roger in Calabria in 1061 and invited the Normans to intervene, helping them take Messina.

ishaq-ibn-ismail.s: Ishaq ibn Ismail was the Arab emir of Tbilisi in the second quarter of the 9th century. Taking advantage of Abbasid weakness, he ruled almost independently, dominated much of eastern Georgia and defied the caliph's authority.

isawa-castle.s: Isawa Castle was a fortress built in 802 by Sakanoue no Tamuramaro in the Kitakami basin, in present-day Ōshū, Iwate Prefecture, during the wars against the Emishi. Soon afterwards it replaced Taga Castle as headquarters of the Chinjufu, the court's military command in the north.

illyrians.s: The Illyrians were ancient peoples of the western Balkans, living along the eastern Adriatic coast and its hinterland. Divided into many tribes, they formed kingdoms such as that of the Ardiaei under Agron and Queen Teuta, which fought Rome in the 3rd century BCE.

irrua.s: Irrua is a town in Edo State in southern Nigeria, the headquarters of the Esan Central local government area and the seat of one of the Esan chiefdoms ruled by an Onojie. It is known for the Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital, a leading centre for the treatment and study of…

ilshu-iliya.s: Ilshu-iliya was the governor of Eshnunna under the last king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, Ibbi-Sin. Around 2026 BCE, as the empire of Ur disintegrated, he broke away and ruled Eshnunna independently.

ipiq-adad-ii.s: Ipiq-Adad II was a king of Eshnunna in the Diyala region of Mesopotamia in the 19th century BCE. He expanded the power of Eshnunna by conquest, extending its reach along the Tigris and towards the middle Euphrates.

iloilo-city.s: Iloilo City is a port city on the south-east coast of Panay in the western Visayas of the Philippines. Opened to foreign trade in 1855, it prospered in the 19th century as the outlet for sugar from Panay and Negros and for local textiles, and its merchant families led the…

ignaz-seipel.s: Ignaz Seipel was an Austrian Catholic priest and leader of the Christian Social Party who served as chancellor of Austria from 1922 to 1924 and from 1926 to 1929. He stabilised the collapsing currency with a loan arranged through the League of Nations under the Geneva…

ibadism.s: Ibadism is a branch of Islam distinct from both Sunnism and Shiism, which arose in Basra in the late 7th century and is named after the early figure Abd Allah ibn Ibad. It holds that the community should elect a just imam, who may be deposed if he breaks the law.

ipf.s: The Ipf is a hill of 668 metres near Bopfingen on the edge of the Nördlinger Ries in Baden-Württemberg. Its summit was fortified in several prehistoric periods and was an important Celtic princely seat of the late Hallstatt period in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, with…

isenheim-altarpiece.s: The Isenheim Altarpiece is a large folding altarpiece painted by Matthias Grünewald, with carvings by Nikolaus of Haguenau, for the Antonite monastery at Isenheim in Alsace between 1512 and 1516. Its harrowing Crucifixion was made for a hospital that treated sufferers of…

isny-im-allgau.s: Isny im Allgäu is a town in the western Allgäu in Baden-Württemberg that grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in 1096. It bought its freedom from the Truchsesses of Waldburg in 1365 and was a free imperial city until 1803, living from linen weaving and trade with Italy.

iller.s: The Iller is a river that rises near Oberstdorf in the Allgäu Alps and flows north through Kempten to join the Danube at Ulm. For much of its course it forms the border between Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

imperial-court-of-rottweil.s: The Imperial Court of Rottweil was a court of the Holy Roman Empire based in the imperial city of Rottweil, first recorded in the 13th century, which heard cases from much of southern and western Germany on the emperor's authority. Its importance declined after the Imperial…

ikaria.s: Ikaria is a Greek island in the eastern Aegean, west of Samos, named in legend after Icarus, who fell into the sea nearby. Under Ottoman rule from the 16th century, it expelled the Turkish garrison in July 1912 and was briefly the Free State of Icaria before uniting with…

iles-du-salut.s: The Îles du Salut (Salvation Islands) are a group of three small islands, Île Royale, Île Saint-Joseph and Devil's Island, off the coast of French Guiana near Kourou. From 1852 to 1953 they formed part of France's penal colony, with Île Royale as the administrative centre and…

indochina-university.s: Indochina University was the first modern university in French Indochina, founded in Hanoi in 1906 under Governor-General Paul Beau. Closed soon afterwards, it was reorganised from 1917 under Albert Sarraut with schools of medicine, law, pedagogy and other fields, training…

ithaque-department.s: Ithaque was a French department created in 1797 from the central Ionian Islands, formerly Venetian, after the Treaty of Campo Formio. Named after the island of Ithaca, it was centred on Cephalonia and was one of three departments, with Corcyre and Mer-Égée, into which France…

institut-degypte.s: The Institut d'Égypte was a learned society founded in Cairo by Napoleon Bonaparte in August 1798 to study Egypt's history, natural history and society, on the model of the Institut de France. Its members, scholars who accompanied the French expedition, prepared the…

istiqlal-party.s: The Istiqlal ('Independence') Party is a Moroccan nationalist party founded in 1944, when it issued a manifesto demanding independence from France and Spain. Led by Allal al-Fassi and Ahmed Balafrej, it worked with Sultan Muhammad V and led the struggle that ended the…

inhambane.s: Inhambane is a port town on a sheltered bay on the coast of southern Mozambique. Vasco da Gama called there in 1498, and Portuguese traders were active in the 16th century, dealing in ivory and later in slaves.

ismet-inonu.s: İsmet İnönü was a Turkish general and statesman, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's closest ally. He won the battles of İnönü against the Greeks in 1921, from which he took his surname, negotiated the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, was prime minister for most of 1923–1937 and succeeded…

ivan-i-of-moscow.s: Ivan I Danilovich, called Kalita ('moneybag'), was Prince of Moscow from 1325 and Grand Prince of Vladimir from 1328 until his death in 1340. He helped the Golden Horde crush the Tver rising of 1327, gained the right to collect the Mongol tribute from other princes, and had…

ilanz.s: Ilanz is a small town on the Vorderrhein in the Surselva region of Graubünden, Switzerland, often called the first town on the Rhine. It was the meeting place of the Grey League and one of the towns where the diet of the Three Leagues met in turn.

incawasi.s: Incawasi is an Inca archaeological site in the Cañete valley of Peru, built in the later 15th century during the war against the coastal lordship of Guarco. According to the chroniclers, Túpac Inca Yupanqui built it as a 'new Cusco' to serve as his base in the campaign.

ibn-khaldun.s: Ibn Khaldun was an Arab historian and thinker born in Tunis in 1332 to a family of Andalusi origin. He served rulers in Tunis, Fez and Granada before writing his universal history, whose introduction, the Muqaddimah, explains the rise and fall of dynasties through asabiyya, or…

isparta.s: Isparta is a city in the Lakes Region of south-western Turkey, capital of the province of the same name. In the 14th century it was one of the main towns of the Hamidid beylik, the Turkmen principality that ruled the lake district, before passing to the Ottomans.

indra-iii.s: Indra III was the Rashtrakuta emperor of the Deccan from 914 to 929. Around 916 he led a raid into northern India that sacked Kannauj, the capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, forcing its king Mahipala I to flee and hastening the decline of the Pratiharas.

izeh.s: Izeh is a city in the Zagros Mountains of Khuzestan province, south-western Iran. Known in the Middle Ages as Idhaj, it was the capital of the Hazaraspid dynasty of Greater Luristan from the 12th to the 15th century.

idrieus.s: Idrieus was satrap of Caria from 351 to 344 BCE, a son of Hecatomnus who succeeded his sister Artemisia II and ruled jointly with his sister and wife Ada. He served the Persian king loyally, sending Carian forces to help recover Cyprus from rebels.

isocrates.s: Isocrates was an Athenian orator and teacher of rhetoric. Around 392 BCE he opened a school in Athens that trained statesmen, historians and orators from across the Greek world.

ishida-mitsunari.s: Ishida Mitsunari was a Japanese warlord and administrator, one of the five commissioners who ran the government of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. After Hideyoshi's death he organised the western coalition against Tokugawa Ieyasu, which was defeated at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

irpinia.s: Irpinia is a mountainous historical region of Campania, southern Italy, largely corresponding to the province of Avellino. Its name recalls the Hirpini, the Samnite people who lived there in antiquity.

italica.s: Italica was a Roman city near modern Santiponce, north of Seville in Spain, founded by Scipio Africanus in 206 BCE for wounded veterans of the Second Punic War. It was the birthplace of the emperor Trajan and probably of Hadrian, who enlarged it with a new quarter, and its…

inge-sargent.s: Inge Sargent is an Austrian-born writer who married Sao Kya Seng, the saopha of the Shan state of Hsipaw, whom she met as a student in the United States. After the 1962 military coup in Burma her husband disappeared in army custody, and she escaped with their daughters.

ifni-war.s: The Ifni War was a conflict of 1957-1958 in which Moroccan irregulars of the Army of Liberation attacked Spanish West Africa, including Ifni and Spanish Sahara. The Spanish were confined to the town of Sidi Ifni until a Franco-Spanish offensive in 1958 restored control in the…

iga-province.s: Iga was an old province of Japan, in the hills south-east of Kyoto, now the western part of Mie Prefecture. In the Sengoku period it had no strong lord and was governed by leagues of local warriors, famous as ninja.

idah.s: Idah is a town in Kogi State, Nigeria, on the east bank of the Niger. It is the capital of the Igala Kingdom and the seat of its ruler, the Attah.

indibilis.s: Indibilis was a chief of the Ilergetes, an Iberian people of the plain around Lleida in north-eastern Spain, during the Second Punic War. With his brother Mandonius he first fought for Carthage, then went over to Scipio Africanus in 209 BCE.

illinois.s: Illinois is a state of the Midwestern United States, lying between Lake Michigan and the Mississippi river, with Springfield as its capital and Chicago as its largest city. Named after the Illinois Confederation, it was part of the French Illinois Country before passing to…

illyria.s: Illyria was the name given by ancient Greek and Roman writers to the western Balkans along the eastern Adriatic, home of the Illyrian peoples. Its kingdoms, notably that of Bardylis and that of the Ardiaean dynasty under Agron, Teuta and Gentius, fought Macedon and Rome until…

imagawa-clan.s: The Imagawa were a Japanese samurai clan, a branch of the Ashikaga founded in the 13th century. From the 14th century they served as shugo governors of Suruga and later Tōtōmi, and in the Sengoku period they became powerful daimyo ruling from Sunpu.

imagawa-yoshitada.s: Imagawa Yoshitada was a Japanese warrior lord and shugo governor of Suruga Province. During the Ōnin War he sided with the eastern army and fought to extend his family's power into Tōtōmi.

imagawa-ujichika.s: Imagawa Ujichika was a Japanese daimyo who ruled Suruga Province from the late 15th century, after his uncle Ise Moritoki, later Hōjō Sōun, helped secure his succession as a boy. He extended Imagawa rule over Tōtōmi and turned the family into a Sengoku warlord house.

imagawa-ujizane.s: Imagawa Ujizane was a Japanese daimyo, son and heir of Imagawa Yoshimoto. After his father's death at Okehazama in 1560 he lost the loyalty of his vassals, and in 1568 and 1569 Takeda Shingen took Sunpu and Tokugawa Ieyasu forced his surrender at Kakegawa Castle, ending the…

inti.s: Inti was the sun god of the Incas and the divine ancestor claimed by the Sapa Inca, the emperor. His chief temple was the Coricancha in Cusco, where a golden image of the sun was kept, and the festival of Inti Raymi was held at the winter solstice in June.

indragiri-hilir-regency.s: Indragiri Hilir is a regency on the east coast of Sumatra in Riau province, Indonesia, covering the lower course and delta of the Indragiri River. Its capital is Tembilahan.

indragiri-hulu-regency.s: Indragiri Hulu is a regency in Riau province on Sumatra, Indonesia, covering the upper course of the Indragiri River. Its capital is Rengat, the former seat of the Indragiri Sultanate.

indragiri-river.s: The Indragiri River rises in the Minangkabau highlands of West Sumatra, where it is called the Kuantan, and flows east through Riau province into the Strait of Malacca. For centuries it carried pepper, gold and forest products from the interior to the coast, and the Indragiri…

ishpakai.s: Ishpakai was the earliest known Scythian king, named in Assyrian texts from the reign of Esarhaddon as ruler of Ishkuza in north-western Iran. He allied with the Mannaeans against Assyria and was killed in battle with the Assyrians around 675 BCE.

international-security-assistance-force.s: The International Security Assistance Force was a multinational military mission in Afghanistan set up by the United Nations Security Council in December 2001, first to secure Kabul. NATO took command in 2003 and extended it across the country, where it fought the Taliban…

iranian-green-movement.s: The Iranian Green Movement was a wave of mass protests that followed the disputed presidential election of June 2009, in which Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner. Supporters of the defeated reformist candidates Mir-Hossein Mousavi and Mehdi Karroubi demonstrated in…

islamic-revolutionary-guard-corps.s: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is a branch of Iran's armed forces founded in 1979 to protect the Islamic Republic and its revolution. Separate from the regular army, it grew powerful during the Iran-Iraq War and controls the Basij militia, ballistic missiles and the…

iskander-mirza.s: Iskander Mirza was a Pakistani soldier and civil servant who became Governor-General in 1955 and the first President of Pakistan in 1956. In October 1958 he abrogated the constitution and declared martial law with army commander Ayub Khan, who deposed him within weeks.

islamabad.s: Islamabad is the capital of Pakistan, a planned city built from the early 1960s at the foot of the Margalla Hills, next to Rawalpindi. Chosen under Ayub Khan to replace Karachi as capital, it was laid out by the Greek planner Constantinos Doxiadis in sectors with green belts.

italo-balbo.s: Italo Balbo was an Italian Fascist leader and aviator, one of the organisers of the March on Rome in 1922. As air minister he led celebrated mass transatlantic flights in 1930–31 and 1933.

italiotes.s: The Italiotes were the Greeks of southern Italy, Magna Graecia, as distinct from the Siceliotes of Sicily. Their colonies, such as Taras, Croton, Sybaris, Locri and Rhegium, were founded from the 8th century BCE.

itza-people.s: The Itza are a Maya people of the Petén lakes in northern Guatemala. Their traditions trace them to Chichen Itza in Yucatán, after whose decline they moved south and founded the kingdom of Nojpetén.

itza-language.s: Itza is a Mayan language of the Yucatecan branch, spoken by the Itza Maya of the Petén lakes in northern Guatemala. Once the language of the kingdom of Nojpetén, it declined under Spanish and Guatemalan rule and is now nearly extinct, with only a few elderly speakers, mainly…

iwellemmeden.s: The Iwellemmeden are a Tuareg confederation of the middle Niger region, in present-day Mali and Niger. They moved into the lands east of the Niger Bend in the 17th century and in the 18th century split into the western Kel Ataram, around Ménaka, and the eastern Kel Dinnik,…

ishikawa-prefecture.s: Ishikawa Prefecture is a prefecture of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast of Honshu, in the Hokuriku region, with its capital at Kanazawa. It covers the old provinces of Kaga and Noto, which formed the core of the Kaga domain of the Maeda clan, the richest domain of the Edo period.

ikko-ikki.s: The Ikkō-ikki were leagues of farmers, local warriors, townspeople and priests belonging to the True Pure Land school of Buddhism in 15th- and 16th-century Japan. In 1488 they overthrew the governor of Kaga and ruled the province until 1580, and from the fortified Ishiyama…

ida-maras.s: Ida-Maras was a district of small kingdoms in the upper Khabur basin of north-eastern Syria, known chiefly from the Mari archives of the 18th century BCE. Its rulers, including the kings of Ashnakkum, Kahat and Ilansura, formed shifting alliances and acknowledged the…

ikkeri.s: Ikkeri is a village in the Shimoga district of Karnataka, India, near Sagar. In the 16th and early 17th centuries it was the capital of the Keladi Nayakas, who served Vijayanagara and then ruled independently, before they moved to Bidanur around 1639.

iferouane.s: Iferouane is an oasis town in the northern Aïr Mountains of Niger. It is a centre of the Kel Ewey Tuareg, with gardens irrigated from wells, and a base for travel into the Aïr and Ténéré.

indira-kala-sangeet-vishwavidyalaya.s: Indira Kala Sangeet Vishwavidyalaya is a university of music, dance and fine arts at Khairagarh in Chhattisgarh, India, founded in 1956. Raja Birendra Bahadur Singh and Rani Padmavati of the former princely state of Khairagarh gave their palace for it and named it after their…

irtysh.s: The Irtysh is a river of Central Asia and Siberia, about 4,250 kilometres long, which rises in the Altai Mountains in China, flows through Kazakhstan and joins the Ob in western Siberia. Its valley was home to steppe peoples such as the Kimek and the Naimans, and Qashliq,…

izates-ii.s: Izates II was king of Adiabene in northern Mesopotamia in the 1st century CE, ruling from Arbela as a vassal of the Parthians. According to Josephus, he and his mother Queen Helena converted to Judaism.

ika-people.s: The Ika are an Igboid-speaking people of Delta State in southern Nigeria, living between Benin City and the Niger around Agbor and Owa. Their language and culture combine Igbo and Edo elements, and several of their kingdoms, including Agbor, had close ties to the Kingdom of…

inishowen.s: Inishowen is the largest peninsula in Ireland, in the north of County Donegal between Lough Swilly and Lough Foyle, ending at Malin Head, the most northerly point of the island. Its name means 'Eógan's island', after the ancestor of the Cenél nEógain, whose royal fort of…

ibrahim-njoya.s: Ibrahim Njoya was king of Bamum in western Cameroon from the late 1880s until 1931. A ruler of wide curiosity, he invented the Bamum script around 1896 and refined it over the following decades, set up schools and a printing press, had maps of his kingdom drawn and devised a…

igun-street.s: Igun Street, or Igun Eronmwon, is the quarter of Benin City in southern Nigeria occupied by the royal guild of bronze casters. For centuries its members made the brass heads, plaques and figures for the Oba's court using the lost-wax method.

ida-of-bernicia.s: Ida was the first known king of Bernicia in north-eastern England. According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle he began to reign in 547 and built the fortress of Bamburgh on the Northumberland coast, which became the dynasty's chief seat.

isidore-of-charax.s: Isidore of Charax was a Greek geographer of the late 1st century BCE or early 1st century CE, from Charax Spasinou in Characene. His surviving Parthian Stations describes the caravan route from Antioch across Mesopotamia and Iran to Arachosia, listing its stopping places and…

ivan-mazuranic.s: Ivan Mažuranić was a Croatian poet, lawyer and politician who served as ban of Croatia from 1873 to 1880, the first ban not of noble birth. His epic poem The Death of Smail-aga Čengić (1846) is a classic of Croatian literature.

imar.s: Ímar was a Viking king of Dublin who appears in the Irish annals from 857, often acting with Amlaíb Conung. Together they took Dumbarton Rock in 870, and at his death in 873 he was called king of the Norsemen of all Ireland and Britain.

ipswich.s: Ipswich is the county town of Suffolk, England, at the head of the Orwell estuary. Founded in the early 7th century as a trading settlement under the East Anglian kings, it is one of the oldest continuously occupied towns of Anglo-Saxon England, and its kilns produced Ipswich…

ipswich-massachusetts.s: Ipswich is a town on the North Shore of Massachusetts, founded by English Puritans in 1634. In 1687 its townspeople, led by the minister John Wise, refused to pay taxes imposed by Governor Edmund Andros without an elected assembly, and their leaders were tried and punished.

ile-de-france.s: Île-de-France is the region around Paris in northern France and the historic heart of the French monarchy. Under the early Capetian kings the royal domain consisted chiefly of this area and Orléans, from which royal power gradually expanded over the kingdom.

illtud.s: Illtud was a British abbot of around 500, founder of the monastic school of Llanilltud Fawr, now Llantwit Major, in Glamorgan. Early saints' lives make him the teacher of Samson of Dol, Gildas and other Welsh saints, and his school became a leading centre of learning in early…

iyasu-v.s: Iyasu V, known as Lij Iyasu, was the uncrowned emperor of Ethiopia from 1913 to 1916, grandson and designated heir of Menelik II. His suspected leanings towards Islam and the Central Powers led the nobility and church to depose him in 1916 in favour of Zewditu, with Ras Tafari…

ioannis-metaxas.s: Ioannis Metaxas was a Greek general and politician who ruled Greece as dictator from 4 August 1936 until his death, with the support of King George II. His regime suspended parliament, imposed censorship and promoted a nationalist Third Hellenic Civilisation.

istvan-szechenyi.s: Count István Széchenyi was a Hungarian reformer and statesman, called 'the greatest Hungarian' by his rival Lajos Kossuth. He funded the founding of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1825, promoted steam navigation on the Danube and the regulation of the Tisza, and…

istvan-bethlen.s: Count István Bethlen was prime minister of Hungary from 1921 to 1931. A Transylvanian aristocrat, he stabilised the post-war kingdom under Regent Horthy, restored open voting in the countryside, obtained a League of Nations loan and sought allies, notably Italy, for revising…

inisfallen.s: Inisfallen is an island in Lough Leane, the Lower Lake of Killarney, in County Kerry, Ireland. A monastery was founded there, by tradition by Saint Finian the Leper in the 7th century, and it became a centre of learning where the Annals of Inisfallen were kept.

idalion-tablet.s: The Idalion Tablet is a bronze plaque of the early 5th century BCE from Idalion in Cyprus, inscribed in Greek in the Cypriot syllabary. It records a contract by which King Stasicypros and the city granted land to the physician Onasilos and his brothers for treating, without…

isaiah.s: Isaiah was a Hebrew prophet active in Jerusalem in the later 8th century BCE, during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah. He warned against reliance on foreign alliances and, according to the Bible, assured Hezekiah that Jerusalem would survive the…

indra-jatra.s: Indra Jatra is an annual festival in Kathmandu, Nepal, held in late summer or early autumn in honour of the god Indra. Celebrated above all by the Newar people, it includes the raising of a ceremonial pole, masked dances and the chariot procession of the living goddess Kumari,…

iltani.s: Iltani was a queen of Karana in northern Mesopotamia in the 18th century BCE, wife of King Aqba-hammu, who ruled as a vassal of Hammurabi of Babylon. Some 200 tablets from her archive, found at Tell al-Rimah, record her management of textile workshops, grain, staff and estates…

indo-european-languages.s: The Indo-European languages are a family of related languages spoken across Europe and much of western and southern Asia, descended from a reconstructed ancestor, Proto-Indo-European, probably spoken in the 4th millennium BCE. Its branches include Germanic, Romance, Celtic,…

icel.s: Icel is the ancestor from whom the kings of Mercia traced their descent in Anglo-Saxon genealogies, which make him a descendant of the continental Anglian king Offa of Angel. He may have led Angles across the North Sea in the late 5th or early 6th century, but nothing is known…

iestyn-ap-gwrgant.s: Iestyn ap Gwrgant was the last native king of Morgannwg, or Glamorgan, in south-east Wales in the late 11th century. Around 1090 he was overthrown by the Norman Robert Fitzhamon, who built a castle at Cardiff and created the marcher Lordship of Glamorgan.

idrimi.s: Idrimi was king of Alalakh in the Amuq plain in the 15th century BCE, a refugee prince from Aleppo who took power with the help of Habiru warriors and ruled as a vassal of Mitanni. His life story is inscribed on a seated statue found at Alalakh in 1939 and now in the British…

imbangala.s: The Imbangala were bands of warriors in 16th- and 17th-century Angola, organised by initiation rather than kinship and bound by strict military laws called kijila. They allied at times with the Portuguese, raiding for captives for the Atlantic slave trade, and also served…

intendancy-of-guadalajara.s: The Intendancy of Guadalajara was an administrative division of New Spain created in 1786 under the Bourbon Reforms, which replaced the older kingdom of New Galicia with intendancies run by royal officials. Governed from Guadalajara, it covered roughly the modern states of…

igbo-people.s: The Igbo are one of the largest ethnic groups of Africa, living mainly in south-eastern Nigeria and speaking the Igbo language. Historically most Igbo communities governed themselves through village assemblies, age grades and title societies rather than kingdoms, though Nri…

igboland.s: Igboland is the homeland of the Igbo people in south-eastern Nigeria, lying mostly east of the lower Niger and extending into the Niger Delta hinterland. It covers forest and savanna country and today spans Anambra, Enugu, Imo, Abia and Ebonyi states and parts of Delta and…

igbo-ukwu.s: Igbo-Ukwu is a town in Anambra State, Nigeria, where excavations by Thurstan Shaw in 1959–64 uncovered elaborate bronze castings, glass beads and a burial of a high-status figure. Dated to the 9th and 10th centuries, the lost-wax bronzes are among the oldest and most intricate…

imo-river.s: The Imo River is a river of south-eastern Nigeria, about 240 km long, that flows through Igboland to the Atlantic near Opobo. In the 19th century it was a key route for palm oil from the Igbo interior to the coast.

istakhr.s: Istakhr was an ancient city in Fars, south-western Iran, a few kilometres north of Persepolis. After the Achaemenid period it became the main city of Persis, and in the early 3rd century CE it was the home of the Sasanian family, whose temple of Anahita stood there.

ion-antonescu.s: Ion Antonescu was a Romanian army officer who ruled Romania as Conducător from 1940 to 1944. Appointed prime minister by Carol II in 1940, he forced the king's abdication, crushed the Iron Guard in 1941 and took Romania into the war against the Soviet Union as an ally of…

iaudas.s: Iaudas was a Berber king of the Aurès mountains in the 530s who resisted the Byzantine reconquest of North Africa. He raided Byzantine Numidia and withstood the first expeditions against him, but in 539 the general Solomon stormed his mountain strongholds and he fled to…

iberians.s: The Iberians were the pre-Roman peoples of the eastern and southern Iberian Peninsula, among them the Turdetani, Edetani and Ilergetes. They spoke a non-Indo-European language written in their own scripts, lived in fortified towns and produced sculpture such as the Lady of Elche.

ishkhani.s: Ishkhani is a medieval Georgian monastery and cathedral in the historic region of Tao, today the village of İşhan in Artvin Province, north-eastern Turkey. Founded in the 7th century, it was rebuilt in the 9th century and given a new dome in the 11th under Bagratid patronage,…

isle-of-wight.s: The Isle of Wight is an island in the English Channel off the coast of Hampshire, known to the Romans as Vectis. Bede records that it was settled by Jutes, and it was conquered by Caedwalla of Wessex in 686.

isle-of-lewis.s: The Isle of Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris, the largest island of the Outer Hebrides in Scotland, with Stornoway as its main town. It holds the Calanais standing stones, and the Lewis chessmen, carved from walrus ivory in the 12th century, were found there in…

isle-of-skye.s: The Isle of Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides off the west coast of Scotland, known for the Cuillin mountains. Under Norse rule until 1266, it was later divided between the MacLeods of Dunvegan and the MacDonalds.

iona.s: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off the west coast of Mull in Scotland. Columba founded a monastery there in 563, which became the head of a network of churches and the centre of the mission to the Picts and Northumbria; the Book of Kells was probably begun there.

ishme-dagan-i.s: Ishme-Dagan I was the elder son of Shamshi-Adad I, the Amorite ruler of the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, in the 18th century BCE. His father installed him as king at Ekallatum on the Tigris while his brother Yasmah-Addu ruled at Mari.

isputahsu.s: Isputahsu was a king of Kizzuwatna in south-eastern Anatolia around the 15th century BCE and one of the first known rulers of that kingdom. He styled himself Great King on his seal.

izborsk.s: Izborsk is an old village in Pskov Oblast, Russia, near the Estonian border, and one of the oldest towns of the Rus'. The Primary Chronicle names it among the towns of the Krivichs and as the seat of Truvor, a brother of Rurik.

iluro.s: Iluro was a Roman town on the site of modern Mataró, on the Maresme coast north-east of Barcelona. Founded in the early 1st century BCE in the territory of the Iberian Laietani, it took its name from an earlier Iberian settlement nearby and became a centre of wine production.

ise-bay.s: Ise Bay is an inlet of the Pacific Ocean on the south coast of central Honshu, Japan, bordered by Aichi and Mie prefectures. It receives the Kiso, Nagara and Ibi rivers, and the port of Nagoya lies at its head.

izu-province.s: Izu Province was an old province of Japan covering the Izu Peninsula and the Izu Islands, now part of Shizuoka Prefecture and Tokyo. Minamoto no Yoritomo lived there in exile before raising his revolt in 1180.

issa-dalmatia.s: Issa was an ancient Greek city on the island of Vis in the central Adriatic, now in Croatia. Founded with the backing of Dionysius I of Syracuse in the early 4th century BCE, it planted its own settlements on the mainland, such as Tragurion (Trogir) and Epetion.

ingauni.s: The Ingauni were a Ligurian people of the western Riviera of Italy, centred on Albium Ingaunum, modern Albenga. They allied with Mago, Hannibal's brother, during the Second Punic War and were defeated by the Romans under Lucius Aemilius Paullus in 181 BCE.

intemelii.s: The Intemelii were a Ligurian people of the western Riviera, on the modern border between France and Italy. Their chief town, Albintimilium, is modern Ventimiglia, whose name preserves theirs.

imbros.s: Imbros (Turkish: Gökçeada) is an island in the northern Aegean Sea near the entrance to the Dardanelles, now part of Turkey. Held in antiquity mostly by Athens and later by Byzantium, the Gattilusi lords of Lesbos and Ainos, and from the 15th century the Ottomans, it had a…

imola.s: Imola is a town in Emilia-Romagna, northern Italy, on the Via Emilia between Bologna and Faenza. Ruled in the late Middle Ages by local lords and at times by the Manfredi of Faenza, it was given by Pope Sixtus IV to his nephew Girolamo Riario in 1473.

isabel-de-clare-4th-countess-of-pembroke.n: Isabel de Clare, 4th Countess of Pembroke
isabel-de-clare-4th-countess-of-pembroke.s: Isabel de Clare was the daughter and heiress of Richard de Clare, called Strongbow, and Aoife, daughter of King Diarmait Mac Murchada of Leinster. Her marriage in 1189 to William Marshal brought him the lordship of Leinster and the earldom of Pembroke.

isabella-of-villehardouin.s: Isabella of Villehardouin was Princess of Achaea from 1289 to 1307, heiress of William II of Villehardouin. Married first to Philip of Anjou, son of Charles I of Naples, she was invested with the principality on her marriage to Florent of Hainaut, and in 1301 married Philip of…

inferno-dante.s: Inferno is the first part of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, written in the early 14th century. It describes Dante's journey, guided by the Roman poet Virgil, through the nine circles of Hell, where he meets sinners from history and from the Italian politics of his day.

islay.s: Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides of Scotland. In the early Middle Ages it was the home of the Cenél nÓengusa of Dál Riata, and from the 14th century it was the heart of the Lordship of the Isles, ruled from Finlaggan.

iftikhar-hussain-khan-mamdot.s: Iftikhar Hussain Khan Mamdot was a Pakistani politician from the family of the nawabs of Mamdot, among the largest landowners of the Punjab. A leader of the Punjab Muslim League, he became the first chief minister of West Punjab after independence in 1947, serving until 1949,…

iron-curtain.s: The Iron Curtain was the political, military and physical boundary that divided Europe after the Second World War, separating the Soviet Union and the communist states of Central and Eastern Europe from the West. The phrase was made famous by Winston Churchill in a speech at…

iranzu.s: Iranzu was a king of Mannaea, south of Lake Urmia in north-western Iran, in the late 8th century BCE. He was a loyal vassal of Sargon II of Assyria, who supported him against rebels backed by Urartu.

izirtu.s: Izirtu, also written Zirta, was the capital of the kingdom of Mannaea in north-western Iran, named in Assyrian royal inscriptions of the 9th to 7th centuries BCE, which record Assyrian armies attacking it. Its location has not been securely identified; proposals include the…

isere-river.s: The Isère is a river in south-eastern France, about 286 kilometres long, which rises in the Alps near the Italian border and flows through the Tarentaise valley and past Grenoble to join the Rhône north of Valence. In antiquity its valleys were home to Alpine and Gallic…

igihalkid-dynasty.s: The Igihalkid dynasty ruled Elam from about 1400 to 1210 BCE, opening the Middle Elamite period. Named after its founder Igi-halki, it consolidated the kingdom of Susa and Anshan, used the Elamite language in royal inscriptions and married into the Kassite royal house of Babylon.

itjtawy.s: Itjtawy, short for Amenemhat-itj-tawy, 'Amenemhat seizes the Two Lands', was the royal capital of Egypt in the Twelfth and Thirteenth Dynasties. It was founded by Amenemhat I around 1980 BCE near Lisht, at the entrance to the Faiyum, moving government from Thebes back towards…

ihya-al-muluk.s: The Ihya al-Muluk is a Persian chronicle of Sistan written in the early 17th century by Malik Shah Husayn Sistani, a member of the region's local ruling family. It traces the history of Sistan from legendary times to the author's own day, with particular detail on the…

ibaraki-prefecture.s: Ibaraki Prefecture is a prefecture of Japan in the Kanto region, north-east of Tokyo, with its capital at Mito. It was formed in 1871 and enlarged in 1875 from the former Mito domain and other domains of Hitachi and Shimosa provinces after the abolition of the han system.

iwate-prefecture.s: Iwate Prefecture is a prefecture in the Tōhoku region of northern Honshu, Japan, with its capital at Morioka. It is the second-largest prefecture by area, mountainous and thinly populated, with the Kitakami river valley and the rugged Sanriku coast.

indian-institute-of-science.s: The Indian Institute of Science is a research university in Bengaluru, India, founded in 1909. It was created with an endowment from the industrialist Jamsetji Tata, with land and support from the Maharaja of Mysore and the Government of India.

ijaw-people.s: The Ijaw are a people of the Niger delta in southern Nigeria, living mostly in Bayelsa, Rivers and Delta states and numbering several million. Fishermen and traders of the creeks and mangrove swamps, they founded city-states such as Nembe, Bonny, Kalabari and Okrika, which…

ibo-island.s: Ibo is a small island of the Quirimbas archipelago off Cabo Delgado province in northern Mozambique. Settled by the Portuguese, it became a fortified town in the late 18th century, the capital of the Cabo Delgado district and a centre of the slave and ivory trade.

inuit.s: The Inuit are the Indigenous peoples of the Arctic of Greenland, Canada and Alaska, speaking languages of the Eskimo-Aleut family. Descendants of the Thule culture, which spread east from Alaska from around 1000 CE, they reached Greenland in the 13th century, where they met…

ivan-sorokin.s: Ivan Sorokin was a Kuban Cossack officer and Red commander in the Russian Civil War. In 1918 he commanded the Red Army of the North Caucasus against Denikin's Volunteer Army.

inaba-province.s: Inaba Province was an old province of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast, corresponding to the eastern part of present-day Tottori Prefecture. In the Edo period it formed, with neighbouring Hōki, the Tottori Domain of the Ikeda family.

imhotep.s: Imhotep was a high official of the Egyptian king Djoser of the Third Dynasty in the 27th century BCE and, by tradition, the architect of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. His name and titles appear on the base of a statue of Djoser.

itsukushima.s: Itsukushima, popularly known as Miyajima, is an island in Hiroshima Bay in the Inland Sea of Japan. It is famous for the Itsukushima Shrine, rebuilt by Taira no Kiyomori in the 12th century, whose great torii gate appears to float at high tide.

iskandar-thani.s: Iskandar Thani was sultan of Aceh from 1636 to 1641. A prince of Pahang brought to Aceh after Iskandar Muda conquered his homeland, he married the sultan's daughter and was chosen as his successor.

ibn-tufayl.s: Ibn Tufayl was an Andalusian philosopher, physician and court official of the Almohad Caliphate, born near Granada. Serving as physician and vizier to the caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf I, he introduced Averroes to the court and encouraged him to write his commentaries on Aristotle.

isthmian-games.s: The Isthmian Games were one of the four Panhellenic festivals of ancient Greece, held every two years near Corinth in honour of Poseidon, with victors crowned with pine or wild celery. In 196 BCE the Roman general Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greek…

infamous-decade.s: The Infamous Decade is the name given to the period of Argentine history from the coup of 1930 to the military revolution of 1943. Conservative governments kept power through systematic electoral fraud while managing the effects of the Great Depression, including the…

isabel-peron.s: Isabel Perón is the third wife of Juan Perón, elected his vice-president in 1973, who succeeded him on his death in July 1974 and became the world's first woman to hold the title of president. Her government was marked by inflation, strikes and the death squads of the…

ictinus.s: Ictinus was a Greek architect of the fifth century BCE who designed the Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens together with Callicrates, under the direction of Pericles and Phidias. Ancient writers also connect him with the hall of the mysteries at Eleusis and the temple of…

ignaz-semmelweis.s: Ignaz Semmelweis was a Hungarian physician who, working at the Vienna General Hospital in 1847, showed that childbed fever was greatly reduced when doctors washed their hands in chlorinated lime before examining women in labour. His findings were widely rejected in his…

imperial-royal-landwehr.s: The Imperial-Royal Landwehr was the territorial army of the Austrian half of Austria-Hungary, created in 1869 after the Compromise of 1867 alongside the joint Imperial and Royal Army and the Hungarian Honvéd. At first a reserve force, it became a full front-line army before…

isonokami-shrine.s: Isonokami Shrine is a Shinto shrine in Tenri, Nara Prefecture, one of the oldest in Japan. It was associated with the Mononobe clan, who kept the Yamato court's weapons, and served as an armoury of sacred swords.

islam-shah-suri.s: Islam Shah Suri was the second ruler of the Sur Empire in northern India, reigning from 1545 to 1554 after his father Sher Shah Suri. He kept his father's administration together and strengthened central control over the Afghan nobles.

ibrahim-adil-shah-i.s: Ibrahim Adil Shah I ruled the Bijapur Sultanate from 1534 to 1558, after the brief reign of his brother Mallu Adil Shah. Breaking with his predecessors, he adopted Sunni Islam, favoured the Deccani nobility over Persian immigrants and replaced Persian with local languages in…

ismail-adil-shah.s: Ismail Adil Shah was the second Adil Shahi sultan of Bijapur, succeeding his father Yusuf Adil Shah in 1510 and ruling until 1534. Like his father he favoured Shia Islam and Persian immigrants at court.

irineu-evangelista-de-sousa-viscount-of-.n: Irineu Evangelista de Sousa, Viscount of Mauá
irineu-evangelista-de-sousa-viscount-of-.s: Irineu Evangelista de Sousa, Viscount of Mauá, was a Brazilian industrialist, banker and entrepreneur. He built Brazil's first railway, opened near Rio de Janeiro in 1854, and invested in shipyards, gas lighting, steamship lines and banks in Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina.

indian-councils-act-1861.s: The Indian Councils Act 1861 was a British law that reorganised the government of British India after the rebellion of 1857. It added non-official members, including some Indians, to the Viceroy's council for legislative business, restored law-making powers to the presidencies…

indian-councils-act-1909.s: The Indian Councils Act 1909, known as the Morley–Minto reforms after the Secretary of State John Morley and the Viceroy Lord Minto, enlarged the legislative councils of British India and introduced indirect election for many of their members. It also created separate…

izz-al-dawla.s: Izz al-Dawla Bakhtiyar was the Buyid ruler of Iraq from 967 to 978, succeeding his father Mu'izz al-Dawla. His weak rule in Baghdad was undermined by conflict between Daylamite and Turkish troops, and a mutiny led by the Turkish commander Sabuktakin in 974 brought his cousin…

ittobaal-of-byblos.s: Ittobaal was a king of Byblos, the son of King Ahiram. He is known from the inscription he had carved on his father's stone sarcophagus, found in 1923, which warns against disturbing the tomb.

insulin.s: Insulin is the hormone that regulates blood sugar, and its absence or failure causes diabetes. It was isolated at the University of Toronto in 1921–1922 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best, with J.

ion-of-chios.s: Ion of Chios was a Greek poet and prose writer of the fifth century BCE who spent much of his life in Athens. He wrote tragedies, lyric poetry and a work of reminiscences describing meetings with Sophocles, Pericles and Cimon, one of the earliest examples of memoir in Greek.

ionians.s: The Ionians were one of the main groups of the ancient Greeks, speaking the Ionic dialect and living in Attica, Euboea, the Cyclades and, from about 1000 BCE, the central west coast of Asia Minor, known as Ionia. Their twelve cities there, including Miletus, Samos and Chios,…

immigration-restriction-act-1901.s: The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 was among the first laws of the new Australian federal parliament and the legal basis of the White Australia policy. It allowed officials to exclude migrants by a dictation test of fifty words in any European language, used to keep out…

international-association-of-the-congo.s: The International Association of the Congo was an organisation controlled by Leopold II of Belgium through which Henry Morton Stanley built stations along the Congo River and collected treaties from local rulers. Presented as a philanthropic and scientific body, it was…

imperial-flanders.s: Imperial Flanders was the part of the County of Flanders east of the Scheldt that the counts held as a fief of the Holy Roman Empire rather than of the French crown. Acquired by Baldwin IV and Baldwin V in the eleventh century, it included the Land of Aalst and the Four Offices.

ivan-vyhovsky.s: Ivan Vyhovsky was hetman of the Zaporozhian Host from 1657 to 1659, after the death of Bohdan Khmelnytsky. Seeking to free Cossack Ukraine from Muscovite control, he concluded the Treaty of Hadiach with Poland-Lithuania in 1658 and, with Crimean allies, defeated a Russian army…

islam-iii-giray.s: Islam III Giray was khan of Crimea from 1644 to 1654. In 1648 he allied with Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossack uprising against Poland-Lithuania, and Tatar forces helped win the battles of Zhovti Vody and Korsun, but he repeatedly made his own terms with the Poles and withdrew at…

iglesias.s: Iglesias is a town in south-western Sardinia, Italy, at the centre of the island's main silver and lead mining district. Founded in the thirteenth century by the Pisan counts of Donoratico under the name Villa di Chiesa, it had its own statutes and mint.

inner-hebrides.s: The Inner Hebrides are the islands off the west coast of mainland Scotland, including Skye, Mull, Islay, Jura, Iona and Tiree. In the early Middle Ages they belonged largely to the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata, and Iona became a centre of Celtic Christianity.

ingelheim-am-rhein.s: Ingelheim am Rhein is a town in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, on the Rhine west of Mainz. Charlemagne built a palace there in the late eighth century, and it was a frequent seat of Carolingian and Ottonian assemblies and synods; in 788 an assembly at Ingelheim condemned Duke…

ivo-of-kermartin.s: Ivo of Kermartin, known as Saint Yves, was a Breton priest and church judge of the diocese of Tréguier, famed for defending the poor without fee. He died in 1303 and was canonised in 1347.

il-caffe.s: Il Caffè was a periodical produced in Milan from June 1764 to May 1766 by Pietro Verri, his brother Alessandro and their circle, including Cesare Beccaria. Modelled on English journals such as The Spectator, it discussed economics, law, science and literature in a lively style.

italian-enlightenment.s: The Italian Enlightenment was the eighteenth-century movement of reform-minded thinkers in the Italian states, centred especially on Milan and Naples. Writers such as Pietro Verri, Cesare Beccaria, Antonio Genovesi and Gaetano Filangieri applied reason to economics, law and…

italic-league.s: The Italic League was an alliance concluded in 1454–1455 by Venice, Milan and Florence, and joined by the Papacy and the Kingdom of Naples, following the Peace of Lodi. Its members promised to defend one another and the existing borders for twenty-five years.

indonesian-national-party.s: The Indonesian National Party (PNI) was founded by Sukarno and others in Bandung on 4 July 1927 to win independence through mass non-cooperation with the Dutch. The colonial government arrested Sukarno in 1929, and the party dissolved itself in 1931.

ibbit-lim.s: Ibbit-Lim was a king of Ebla in the early second millennium BCE, when the city had revived under Amorite rule. He is known from the inscribed basalt torso of a votive statue found at Tell Mardikh in 1968 by the Italian excavators led by Paolo Matthiae.

ibbi-zikir.s: Ibbi-Zikir was a vizier of the kingdom of Ebla in the twenty-fourth century BCE, the son and successor of the vizier Ibrium. Serving under King Ishar-Damu in the last years before the palace was destroyed, he appears in the archives directing the administration and leading…

iblul-il.s: Iblul-Il was a king of Mari on the Euphrates in the twenty-fourth century BCE. A letter found at Ebla records his campaigns against towns in Ebla's sphere along the middle Euphrates and in northern Syria, after which Ebla paid tribute to Mari.

igrish-halam.s: Igrish-Halam was a king of Ebla in the twenty-fourth century BCE and one of the earliest rulers documented in the archives of its palace. During his reign Ebla was under pressure from Mari, to which it delivered heavy payments of silver and gold.

irkab-damu.s: Irkab-Damu was a king of Ebla in the twenty-fourth century BCE and successor of Igrish-Halam. During his reign Ebla began to recover from Mari's dominance, building alliances and extending its control over neighbouring towns, and the treaty with Abarsal may date from this period.

ishar-damu.s: Ishar-Damu was the last king of Ebla documented in the archives of its palace, reigning in the twenty-fourth century BCE. He came to the throne young, and his viziers Ibrium and Ibbi-Zikir directed much of the government and led its wars, including a conflict with Mari.

ishkhara.s: Ishkhara was a goddess of the ancient Near East, worshipped at Ebla in Syria from the third millennium BCE and later in Mesopotamia and among the Hurrians and Hittites. She was associated with love and with oaths, and she appears among the divine witnesses of treaties.

ismail-ii-of-granada.s: Ismail II was Nasrid emir of Granada from August 1359 to June 1360. He came to power in a palace coup that deposed his half-brother Muhammad V, but within a year he was overthrown and killed by his kinsman and former supporter, who took the throne as Muhammad VI.

inukai-tsuyoshi.s: Inukai Tsuyoshi was a Japanese party politician and Prime Minister from December 1931 to May 1932. A long-serving member of the Diet and leader of the Rikken Seiyūkai, he resisted military control of policy and sought a negotiated settlement in Manchuria.

iwakura-mission.s: The Iwakura Mission was a Japanese embassy that toured the United States and Europe from 1871 to 1873, led by Iwakura Tomomi with Kido Takayoshi, Ōkubo Toshimichi and Itō Hirobumi. It failed to revise the unequal treaties, but it studied Western government, industry, education…

ivan-vladislav.s: Ivan Vladislav (died 1018) was the last tsar of the First Bulgarian Empire, ruling from 1015 to 1018. A nephew of Samuel, whose life had been spared at Gavril Radomir's request when his father Aron was killed, he seized the throne by murdering Gavril Radomir.

iyasu-ii.s: Iyasu II was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1730 to 1755, ruling for much of his reign under the regency of his mother, Empress Mentewab. His court at Gondar was a centre of building and painting.

idrija.s: Idrija is a town in western Slovenia, the site of one of the world's largest mercury mines, discovered around 1490 and worked for some five centuries. Under the Habsburgs from 1509 it was a major source of royal revenue, and its mercury was used in Spanish America to refine…

ibn-al-abbar.s: Ibn al-Abbar was an Andalusi scholar, poet and historian from Valencia who served as secretary to its Muslim rulers and, after the city fell to Aragon in 1238, to the Hafsid sultans in Tunis. He wrote a famous poem appealing to Abu Zakariya Yahya for help for Valencia and…

ibn-arafa.s: Ibn Arafa was a jurist of the Maliki school from Tunis, the leading religious scholar of the Hafsid capital in the fourteenth century. He served as imam of the Zaytuna Mosque and mufti of Tunis, and his works on Maliki law, especially his concise legal compendium, were studied…

ibn-tafrakin.s: Ibn Tafrakin was a chamberlain, or hajib, of the Hafsid sultanate and the dominant figure in Tunis in the mid-fourteenth century. After the Marinid occupation of Tunis ended, he governed in the name of the young sultan Abu Ishaq II, whom he had placed on the throne, until his…

institutio-oratoria.s: The Institutio Oratoria is a twelve-book Latin treatise on the education and training of the orator, written by Quintilian, a rhetorician from Calagurris in Hispania, around 95 CE. It covers a speaker's schooling from childhood and the theory and practice of rhetoric.

inca-garcilaso-de-la-vega.s: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega was a writer born in Cusco to a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman of the royal family. Settling in Spain in 1560, he wrote the Comentarios Reales de los Incas, published in 1609, a history of the Incas and the Spanish conquest.

inkallajta.s: Inkallajta is an Inca archaeological site in the Cochabamba Department of Bolivia, on the eastern frontier of the empire, built in the late 15th century. Its walled complex includes one of the largest roofed halls, or kallanka, of the Inca world.

inti-raymi.s: Inti Raymi, the Festival of the Sun, was the main religious festival of the Inca Empire, held in Cusco at the June solstice in honour of the sun god Inti. Banned by the Spanish authorities in the 16th century, it was revived as a public spectacle in 1944 and is now staged each…

indonesian-national-armed-forces.s: The Indonesian National Armed Forces (Tentara Nasional Indonesia, TNI) are the army, navy and air force of Indonesia. They grew out of the militias and security forces formed in 1945 to fight the returning Dutch, and 5 October is kept as Armed Forces Day.

ibrahim-iskandar-of-johor.s: Ibrahim Iskandar is the Sultan of Johor, who succeeded his father in 2010, and the King of Malaysia. Under Malaysia's system of rotating monarchy the Conference of Rulers elected him the seventeenth Yang di-Pertuan Agong, and he took office on 31 January 2024 for a five-year…

imo-incident.s: The Imo Incident was a mutiny by unpaid soldiers in Seoul in July 1882. Angered by rice rations that were late and spoiled, and by favour shown to a new Japanese-trained unit, they attacked officials and the Japanese legation, and Queen Min fled the palace.

injo-of-joseon.s: Injo was the sixteenth king of Joseon, ruling from 1623 to 1649. He came to the throne through a coup that deposed his uncle Gwanghaegun and broke with his policy of neutrality towards the Manchus.

igor-svyatoslavich.s: Igor Svyatoslavich was prince of Novgorod-Seversk and, from 1198, of Chernigov. In 1185 he led a raid against the Cumans that ended in disaster: his army was destroyed and he was captured, though he later escaped.

instruction-of-vladimir-monomakh.s: The Instruction of Vladimir Monomakh is a work written by the grand prince of Kiev Vladimir Monomakh, probably in the early twelfth century, as guidance for his sons. It combines advice on the duties of a Christian ruler, such as justice, mercy and keeping one's oath, with an…

iziaslav-i-of-kiev.s: Iziaslav I was grand prince of Kiev and the eldest surviving son of Yaroslav the Wise, succeeding him in 1054. After the Cumans defeated him on the Alta River in 1068 the people of Kiev drove him out; he returned with Polish help, was expelled again by his brothers in 1073 and…

innviertel.s: The Innviertel is a region of Upper Austria between the Inn, the Danube and the Salzach rivers, with towns such as Braunau am Inn and Ried. Part of Bavaria for centuries, it was ceded to Austria by the Treaty of Teschen in 1779.

ius-regale-montanorum.s: The Ius regale montanorum was a mining code issued around 1300 by Wenceslaus II, king of Bohemia, for the silver mines of Kutná Hora. Drafted with the help of the Italian lawyer Gozzius of Orvieto, it regulated mining rights, the work of miners and the royal share of the ore.

isingoma-mpuga-rukidi.s: Isingoma Mpuga Rukidi is remembered in tradition as the first king of the Babito dynasty of Bunyoro-Kitara. The stories present him as a Luo prince from the north who took over the lands of the departed Chwezi, adopted their regalia and rituals and claimed to be their heir;…

isaac-newton.s: Isaac Newton was an English mathematician and physicist, one of the central figures of the Scientific Revolution. In his Principia of 1687 he set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and he also did fundamental work in optics and, independently of Leibniz,…

ioane-petritsi.s: Ioane Petritsi was a Georgian Neoplatonist philosopher and translator of the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries. After working in Byzantium and at the Petritsoni monastery in Bulgaria, he is traditionally said to have taught at the Gelati academy.

ivane-mkhargrdzeli.s: Ivane Mkhargrdzeli was a Georgian-Armenian noble and general of the Zakarid family who, with his brother Zakare, commanded the armies of Queen Tamar. Together they won the victories of Shamkor in 1195 and Basiani around 1202 and conquered much of Armenia, which the family…

iviron-monastery.s: Iviron Monastery is an Eastern Orthodox monastery on Mount Athos in northern Greece, founded around 980 by Georgian monks, John the Iberian and his son Euthymius, with support from the Byzantine emperor. Its name means 'of the Iberians', that is, the Georgians.

international-financial-commission.s: The International Financial Commission was a body of representatives of the great powers set up in 1898 to supervise Greece's public finances. Imposed after Greece's state bankruptcy of 1893 and its defeat in the Greco-Turkish War of 1897, it collected certain state revenues,…

idwal-foel.s: Idwal Foel, meaning 'the bald', was king of Gwynedd from 916 to 942, a grandson of Rhodri the Great. He submitted to the English kings and attended the court of Æthelstan, witnessing his charters.

istvan-werboczy.s: István Werbőczy was a Hungarian jurist and politician who compiled the customary law of the Hungarian nobility in the Tripartitum, presented to the diet in 1514. A leader of the lesser nobility, he briefly served as palatine in 1525 and was later appointed chief judge of the…

irish-house-of-commons.s: The Irish House of Commons was the elected lower house of the Parliament of Ireland, which existed from the Middle Ages until 1800. From the seventeenth century its members were drawn almost entirely from the Protestant landowning class, and Catholics were excluded from…

istituto-per-la-ricostruzione-industrial.s: The Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (IRI) was an Italian state holding company founded in 1933 to rescue banks and industrial firms ruined by the Great Depression. It took controlling stakes in major banks, steel, shipbuilding and engineering, making the Italian…

isidore-of-seville.s: Isidore of Seville was archbishop of Seville from about 600 to 636 and the leading scholar of Visigothic Spain. His Etymologies, an encyclopedia of ancient learning, was one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages, and he also wrote a history of the Goths.

irfan-habib.s: Irfan Habib (born 1931) is an Indian historian of medieval and early modern India, long associated with Aligarh Muslim University. His book The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963) and his Atlas of the Mughal Empire made him one of the leading authorities on Mughal economy…

italian-league.s: The Italian League was a defensive alliance formed in 1454–1455 after the Peace of Lodi between Milan and Venice, joined by Florence, the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples. Its members guaranteed one another's territories for twenty-five years.

ignatius-of-loyola.s: Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556) was a Basque nobleman and soldier who founded the Society of Jesus. Badly wounded defending the citadel of Pamplona against a Franco-Navarrese army in 1521, he underwent a religious conversion during his recovery and wrote the Spiritual Exercises.

iorwerth-ap-bleddyn.s: Iorwerth ap Bleddyn was a prince of Powys, son of Bleddyn ap Cynfyn. In 1102 he deserted Robert of Bellême, Earl of Shrewsbury, for Henry I of England, helping to bring about the earl's fall, but Henry later imprisoned him.

immanuel-kant.s: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher who lived and taught all his life in Königsberg in East Prussia. In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781) and later works he examined the limits of human knowledge and grounded morality in reason through the categorical imperative.

ijwi-island.s: Ijwi Island is a large island in Lake Kivu, part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was home to a small kingdom of the Havu people.

imana.s: Imana is the creator god of the traditional religion of Rwanda and Burundi, a distant supreme being believed to be the source of life and fertility. Imana was thought to be linked with the sacred kingship, and many personal names include the word.

ilsharah-yahdub.s: Ilsharah Yahdub was a king of Saba and Dhu Raydan, ruling from Marib with his brother Ya'zil Bayyin around the late second or early third century CE. Their inscriptions, dedicated at the Awwam temple of Almaqah, record wars against Himyar, Hadramawt and Aksumite forces in…

italian-campaign-of-1796-1797.s: The Italian campaign of 1796–1797 was Napoleon Bonaparte's first great command, in the War of the First Coalition. In April 1796 he knocked the Kingdom of Sardinia out of the war, then defeated the Austrians at Lodi, Arcole and Rivoli and took Mantua.

isthmus-of-panama.s: The Isthmus of Panama is the narrow strip of land between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean that links North and South America. Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed it in 1513, and it became a key route for Spanish silver.

inverness.s: Inverness is a city in the Highlands of Scotland, at the mouth of the River Ness on the Moray Firth. The nearby hill fort of Craig Phadrig and the area around the Ness are associated with the Pictish king Bridei son of Maelchon, whom Columba visited in the 560s.

ibiranu.s: Ibiranu was king of Ugarit in the later thirteenth century BCE, the son of Ammishtamru II. Letters from the Hittite court reproached him for failing to pay homage in person and for neglecting his military obligations, signs of growing strain between Ugarit and its overlord.

ilimilku.s: Ilimilku was a scribe and priest of Ugarit who copied the major mythological and epic texts in Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform, including the Baal cycle and the epics of Kirta and Aqhat. His colophons name him as a pupil of the chief priest Attenu and place his work under a king…

ishpuini.s: Ishpuini was king of Urartu in the late ninth century BCE, the son of Sarduri I. With his son Menua as co-ruler he introduced inscriptions in the Urartian language, organised the state cult of the god Haldi and extended Urartian influence to the sanctuary of Musasir, as…

ivan-mestrovic.s: Ivan Meštrović was a Croatian sculptor and architect, one of the leading sculptors of the twentieth century. A supporter of South Slav unity and a member of the Yugoslav Committee, he created monumental works including the Monument to the Unknown Hero on Mount Avala, the…

ivo-andric.s: Ivo Andrić was a Yugoslav novelist and diplomat born in Bosnia. His novels, above all The Bridge on the Drina (1945), trace the history of Bosnia under Ottoman and Austrian rule.

idomeneus.s: Idomeneus is a Cretan king in Greek mythology, grandson of Minos and ruler of Knossos, who led eighty ships of Cretans to the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad. One of the leading Greek warriors, he was later said to have vowed to sacrifice the first living thing he met on his…

iliad.s: The Iliad is an ancient Greek epic poem attributed to Homer, composed probably in the eighth or seventh century BCE. Set in the tenth year of the Trojan War, it tells of the wrath of Achilles and its consequences, ending with the funeral of Hector.

inthasom.s: Inthasom was king of Luang Phrabang from 1723 to 1749, a grandson of Sourigna Vongsa, the last king of united Lan Xang. With his brother Kingkitsarat he resisted the claims of Sai Ong Hue of Vientiane, and his long reign consolidated the northern kingdom after the division of…

ibn-salim-al-aswani.s: Ibn Salim al-Aswani was an Egyptian official and writer of the 10th century, sent by the Fatimid commander Jawhar as envoy to the king of Makuria around 969. His account of Nubia survives only in quotations by later authors such as al-Maqrizi, and describes a prosperous and…

internal-security-act-1960.s: The Internal Security Act 1960 was a Malaysian law allowing detention without trial, introduced at the end of the Malayan Emergency to fight communist insurgency. It let the government hold people for renewable two-year periods and was used against politicians, activists and…

ibn-hajar-al-asqalani.s: Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani was an Egyptian scholar of hadith and Shafi'i jurist of Mamluk Cairo, where he served several terms as chief judge. His Fath al-Bari, a commentary on the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, became the standard work of its kind, and he also wrote biographical…

investiture-of-zimri-lim.s: The Investiture of Zimri-Lim is a wall painting from the palace of Mari, dating to the reign of Zimri-Lim in the eighteenth century BCE. It shows the king receiving the symbols of kingship from the goddess Ishtar, framed by palm trees, protective deities and mythical creatures.

institutional-revolutionary-party.s: The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) is a Mexican political party that held the presidency without interruption from its founding in 1929 until 2000. Founded by Plutarco Elías Calles as the National Revolutionary Party, reorganised by Lázaro Cárdenas in 1938 and renamed…

instruction-of-amenemhat.s: The Instruction of Amenemhat is an ancient Egyptian literary text of the Twelfth Dynasty in which the dead king Amenemhat I advises his son Senusret I, describing an attack on his life by members of his court. Probably composed early in Senusret's reign, it supported his rule…

insein.s: Insein is a township in the northern part of Yangon, Myanmar. In 1949, early in the Karen insurgency, Karen forces held Insein for more than three months, within a few miles of the capital, before government troops drove them out.

innu.s: The Innu, called Montagnais by the French, are an Indigenous people of eastern Quebec and Labrador in Canada who traditionally lived by hunting caribou and fishing. Their alliance with Samuel de Champlain against the Iroquois, made at Tadoussac in 1603, helped found the French…
